title: 7 Battery-Electric Semi Trucks Hauling Freight in 2026
content:
Automotive & Mobility
Design & Manufacturing
October 9, 2026
7 Slides
Start slideshow
Next-generation Volvo VNL Electric truck
Volvo Trucks North America
For most of the past century, fleet operators relied on diesel trucks to move heavy freight. Then came the late 2010s, when manufacturers first offered battery-electric Class 8 trucks. A step forward, the offerings were still limited in battery capacity and charging speed, ultimately confining them to port drayage and short regional loops.
But over the past two years, engineers have pushed past those limits with larger batteries and faster charging. Manufacturers now sell trucks carrying more than 600 kWh and quote ranges of 500 to 700 kilometers at full gross weight. At the top of that range, a European driver can cover most of a nine-hour legal driving day on one charge.
Truck makers have also started fitting Megawatt Charging System (MCS) connectors to production trucks. With them, drivers can recover several hundred kilometers of range during a mandatory 45-minute rest break.
Given the confluence of these innovations and recent rising diesel costs, trucking companies have begun ordering electric semis in volume this year.
For example, in September, a shipper coalition placed the largest US electric truck order to date.

Why EV Charging Design Is Now a Competitive Advantage for Operators & Manufacturers Alike
With so much excitement in the field, we've put together a list of seven battery-electric semi trucks hauling freight in 2026. Read on to learn about the batteries, ranges, and fleets behind each one.

title: Peak Energy’s Dr. Lucy Li on Sodium-Ion Battery Innovations
content:
Industry Outlook
Lithium-Ion Batteries
Materials
Interviews
Discover Peak Energy’s Dr. Lucy Li insights on sodium-ion batteries, grid modernization, and energy storage innovations at scale.
October 9, 2026
4 Min Read
Peak Energy's 183,000 square foot manufacturing facility in Sacramento.
Peak Energy
Dr. Lucy Li, Staff Technical Program Manager on the Cell Engineering team at Peak Energy, recently shared her expertise in an exclusive Q&A with
Battery Technology
ahead of her appearance at the
Battery Show North America
, where she will speak on the panel
Building the Modern Grid: Storage, Resiliency, and Electrification at Scale
Dr. Li explores the evolving landscape of battery technology, highlighting the unique advantages of sodium-ion systems for grid applications, the challenges of scaling these technologies for commercial deployment, and the strategies Peak Energy uses to enhance grid resiliency and flexibility.
At Peak Energy, you lead Peak Energy’s cell-level development programs for sodium-ion systems. What unique advantages do sodium-ion batteries offer over traditional lithium-ion batteries for modern grid applications, and what common challenges arise when scaling these systems for multi-GWh commercial deployments?
Related:
Battery Show Keynotes Tackle Supply Chains, AI Impact & Manufacturing Scale from Oct. 12-15
Dr. Lucy Li, Staff Technical Program Manager on the Cell Engineering team at Peak Energy:
A lot of people still evaluate batteries through an electric vehicle (EV) lens, where energy density, power, and weight are critical. For grid storage, the priorities are different: lifetime cost, safety, cycle life, reliability, and thermal performance. That’s where sodium-ion makes a lot of sense. Our NFPP and hard-carbon chemistry uses abundant materials and has strong thermal stability, enabling passive cooling and reducing overall system costs.
At multi-GWh scale, a key challenge for any emerging battery technology is coordinating rapid technology development with manufacturing scale-up and supply chain maturity. Sodium-ion has an advantage here: our NFPP/hard-carbon chemistry can leverage existing LFP manufacturing infrastructure with targeted modifications, including switching the anode current collector from copper to aluminum. This compatibility allows us to leverage established manufacturing capabilities and available production capacity, accelerating commercialization while reducing the need for new capital investment.
What specific strategies or innovations does Peak Energy employ to integrate its energy storage systems with renewable energy sources, and how do these systems enhance grid resiliency and flexibility?
At Peak Energy, we design the chemistry and system together to optimize storage for grid performance, reliability, and costs. While battery costs have dropped dramatically, operating and maintaining storage plants are still a significant part of the economics. By eliminating active cooling, our systems remove a major maintenance and failure point while also reducing the energy required to operate the plant.
Related:
Highlights of the Open Tech Forums at The Battery Show North America
The value for renewable projects is not that storage can shift solar and wind, but that our system can do that more efficiently and reliably over its lifetime. Lower auxiliary power, less maintenance, and high availability can improve the economics and useful life of those storage investments. We’re proving that approach in the field with utility and independent power producer partners.
Battery energy storage systems. Courtesy of Young777 / iStock via Getty Images.
What unique challenges do AI-driven data centers present for battery energy storage, and how can these challenges be addressed to ensure scalability and reliability?
AI-driven data centers create large, rapidly growing 24/7 loads, often where grid capacity is constrained. Batteries can help them connect faster by managing their power draw and ensuring they stay within their grid connection limit. That speed to power is increasingly valuable as AI demand grows.
Once operating, efficiency directly impacts revenue because power consumed by the battery system is power that can't be used for productive computing. Traditional BESS designs can require significant power for cooling and other auxiliary loads. Peak Energy’s passively cooled sodium-ion BESS combines high roundtrip efficiency and low auxiliary power draw, leaving more power available for computing. Our simpler system design also means fewer components to maintain or fail, supporting availability and uptime. That’s why data centers are an important focus for us alongside utilities and IPPs.
Related:
Explore the First 15 Years of The Battery Show
As someone deeply involved in both technical development and industry leadership initiatives, how do you see the role of collaboration—across utilities, technology providers, and policymakers—for resilient and reliable energy storage solutions?
No single company can modernize the grid. Utilities bring operational and reliability requirements; technology providers bring new chemistries and system designs; suppliers provide the materials and manufacturing capacity to scale; and policymakers shape areas like interconnection, permitting, and domestic manufacturing.
At Peak, I see collaboration as critical because technology, supply chain, and policy all have to evolve together. As we build toward a more domestic supply chain, policy directly affects how we source, qualify, and collaborate with partners. Through my involvement with the Battery Show advisory board, I also see the value of bringing these different parts of the industry together to share knowledge and accelerate commercialization.
Are there any additional insights, challenges, or opportunities related to energy storage and grid modernization that you feel are important to highlight, but were not covered in the questions above?
Two things stand out. First, building a domestic supply chain requires demand and deployment to grow together. Real projects give cell and materials manufacturers the confidence to scale. Processed battery materials remain a significant gap in the US supply chain and energy security are important reasons to invest in this industry, beyond cell cost alone.
Second, workforce. Scaling energy storage requires engineers, technicians, and program leaders across many disciplines. As Program Director and co-lead of the Volta Foundation’s Women in Batteries initiative, I’ve seen firsthand how important it is to build a strong and diverse talent pipeline. That workforce development is just as important to scaling the industry as the next technical breakthrough.

title: Battery economy creates manufacturing opportunities
content:
Design & Manufacturing
Battery Applications
Interviews
Tom Kelly of Automation Alley discusses how battery demand creates new markets for small manufacturers in defense, robotics, and energy storage.
October 9, 2026
4 Min Read
Automation Alley’s Project DIAMOnD 3D printing initiative in Auburn Hills, MI.
Automation Alley
At a Glance
Small manufacturers can leverage automotive expertise to enter aerospace, defense, and energy markets.
Digital tools like AI and 3D printing help smaller firms compete without massive capital investments.
Adapting operations and investing in workforce skills positions manufacturers for long-term growth.
Tom Kelly, executive director and CEO of
Automation Alley
, has good news for manufacturers at The Battery Show North America. His presentation, “
The Next Industrial Transformation: How Manufacturers Can Win in the Battery Economy and Beyond
,” explores how the global battery revolution is creating opportunities for manufacturers that extend well beyond electric vehicles.
Michigan based Automation Alley is a regional foundation of more than 4,000 member companies spanning all 83 Michigan counties. It unites industry, academia, and government to build a connected ecosystem that drives technological adoption, workforce development, and economic prosperity. Over the past 25 years, its programs have engaged one in three Michigan manufacturers, helping companies of all sizes develop the skills, strategies, and partnerships needed to thrive in a rapidly changing digital landscape.
In his presentation, Kelly will point out that as supply chains evolve and demand accelerates across energy storage, defense, aerospace, medical devices, robotics and other advanced industries, manufacturers of all sizes have an unprecedented opportunity to diversify, innovate and compete in new markets.
Related:
Five Takeaways from Panasonic Energy's New Battery R&D Facility
Automation Alley CEO Tom Kelly. Credit: Automation Alley
I had a few questions for Kelly, which he answered by email:
How Small Manufacturers Can Capitalize on the Battery Economy Beyond EVs
Why should manufacturers view the growing battery economy as an opportunity for broader industrial transformation, rather than just an electric vehicle story?
Automation Alley CEO Tom Kelly:
The battery economy represents much more than the shift to electric vehicles. We're seeing new opportunities across energy storage, defense, aerospace, robotics and other advanced industries, creating possibilities for manufacturers willing to adapt.
However, taking advantage of these opportunities requires more than entering a new market. Manufacturers need to rethink how they operate, embrace digital technologies and build the flexibility required to respond to changing demands. At Automation Alley, our focus is helping small and midsize manufacturers navigate this transformation so they can remain competitive and position themselves for long-term growth.
For small and midsize manufacturers who want to branch out from traditional automotive work, where do you see the best opportunities right now?
Michigan has a strong manufacturing foundation, and many smaller automotive suppliers have capabilities that are transferrable to related industries like aerospace, defense, electric vehicles and advanced energy. The challenge is helping these companies identify where their expertise fits and what they need to do to compete in new markets.
Related:
Results of Donut Lab's Nail Penetration Safety Test
That's part of the focus of the
Michigan Auto Supplier Transition Program
(MAST-P), which provides no-cost support to very small manufacturers connected to the internal combustion engine supply chain. Recently expanded to serve eligible manufacturers across all 83 Michigan counties, the program helps companies strengthen their operations, assess new opportunities and prepare for growth beyond traditional automotive manufacturing. Ultimately, this is about diversification and building more resilient businesses that aren't dependent on a single industry.
Digital transformation strategies for manufacturers entering new markets
What role can advanced manufacturing technologies play in helping smaller manufacturers break into new industries and stay competitive?
Technologies like AI, automation and additive manufacturing are changing what's possible for smaller manufacturers. They can help companies improve efficiency, accelerate product development and expand their capabilities without the level of capital investment or constraints of traditional manufacturing, such as centralized facilities, labor-intensive quality control process and rigid tooling requirements.
Related:
Organic Flow Batteries Meet Steel Tank Infrastructure for Grid-Scale Energy Storage
Our Project DIAMOnD initiative demonstrates this shift in action. Through its distributed 3D printing network and Marketplace, manufacturers can access production capabilities, connect with new customers and put their own equipment and expertise to work. We've also expanded access to industrial 3D printing through our Digital Transformation Center, giving more businesses opportunities to explore and apply additive manufacturing technology. Together, these efforts demonstrate how digital transformation can open new business opportunities and help smaller manufacturers compete in new ways.
What kinds of investments should manufacturers be making today to position themselves for long-term growth?
The most important investment manufacturers can make is in their ability to adapt. That starts with embracing a software-first mindset and identifying where technologies like AI, automation and additive manufacturing can strengthen operations and create new opportunities.
Beyond technology, companies also need to invest in their people, develop new skills and build a culture that's open to innovation and change. Manufacturers don't necessarily need to make massive investments all at once. They can start small, test new approaches and build on what works.
The companies that will be best positioned for the future are those that recognize digital transformation isn't a one-time project. It's an ongoing shift in how they operate, innovate and compete.

title: BYD builds 150,000th commercial NEV – an 800 hp Q3 electric semi truck
content:

Jo Borrás

The BYD Q3 battery-electric semi truck shown here marked a major production milestone this week, becoming the 150,000th new energy commercial vehicle to roll off the assembly line at BYD’s truck plant in Huai’an, Jiangsu province.
Global EV leader BYD has spent years growing its passenger car and battery businesses, and now it’s looking to put that growth mindset to work in the commercial vehicle space, too. Heavy trucks are a critical piece of that puzzle, with HDEVs offering fleet operators a way to dramatically cut diesel consumption and emissions without sacrificing the performance needed to move heavy loads across a continent.
after crossing the 150,000-electrified truck milestone

Big business
BYD puts on an electric truck show.
BYD sold 6,848 NEV trucks in September alone
, up 113.33% year-over-year. That puts the delivery tally at 53,032 units through the first 9 months of 2026 – a number that
CNEVPost
is reporting to be a 28.46% increase compared to 2025.
The Q3 itself pairs 600 kWh’s worth of the company’s familiar blade-style lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery packs with a 600 kW (~800 hp) dual-motor reportedly good enough to haul 108,000 lbs. of gross combined vehicle weight over 325 km away (~200 miles) from where it started on a single charge.
To get the big Q3 back on the move quickly, BYD built-in support for dual-gun DC fast charging, claiming the ability to go from a 20-80% state of charge in just 30 minutes.

title: Battery swap works: Nio completes 1.2 million swaps in a SINGLE WEEK
content:
While oil prices and range anxiety dominate Western EV headlines, Nio’s battery-swap system in China keeps reaching new milestones that prove the technology can rival a traditional refueling infrastructure at scale, performing 1.2 million battery swaps over the holiday.
Nio kicked off this year busting record after record, posting six-figure swap numbers during the third day of the Chinese Lunar New Year celebrations and marking the third such record for Nio in as many days – but the company hasn’t stoped there. New reports indicate the company broke those impressive records again, performing nearly 1.2 million swaps over the National Day celebrations last week.
The Chinese EV brand’s ~4,100 battery swap stations completed 1,192,221 consumer battery swaps from October 1st to 7th, with a daily average nearly 22% higher than the year prior according to a holiday charging and battery swap report released on Friday.
And, from everything we can see, Nio’s swap stations handled the day with exactly the sort of high-tech precision we’ve come to expect from the brand that claims battery swapping, not increasingly faster charging, is the right solution for road tripping travelers.
Life is a highway
Highway travelers accounted for a substantial share of the holiday week’s battery swap demand – and, when measured in terms of energy, that demand was substantial. More than 24.83 million kWh of electricity were turned into efficient, zero-emission travel.
Despite a number of early EV adopters with an overdeveloped concept of ownership, battery swap technology has proven to be both extremely effective and extremely positive to the overall EV ownership experience.
Top comment by Prana686
Would be interested to hear what design constraints the vehicle engineers at Nio must navigate. Are there a handful of battery bolt templates they must design within, or does the system have adaptability for any arrangement within a given footprint? Are the high voltage connectors required to be placed in specific locations? How many different pack sizes are compatible with the existing swap chargers physical storage and electrical capacity?
The speed and convenience is enticing no doubt. My main concern is manufactures each having proprietary stations. Assuming other manufactures began leaning into battery swap, they must create some strict uniformity standards they all have to design around for interoperable battery changers, plus somehow track all the various companies batteries. Or, much more likely, every maker would need their own branded swap stations, and the infrastructure clutter becomes immense.
It's a cool technology, and provides some advantages (even more than speed, battery health tracking and perpetually healthy battery packs is paramount here). That said, I struggle to envision this as a smart widespread approach to be pursued by the industry as a whole. Granted, the heavy vehicle industry is a different story and strikes me as a better use case.
I suspect Nio will face some growing pains in the future though, constrained by their battery swap compatability requirements as they attempt to innovate future vehicle designs. Only time will tell
For drivers, the process is simple: the driver pulls into a swap station, and in three to five minutes leaves with a fully charged battery. No getting out in the rain or snow, no worries about being stuck in an immobilized vehicle if someone’s harassing you outside, no worries about elderly or disabled drivers tripping over charging cables. Multiply that sort of convenience by 175,000 takers in a single day, and what you’re seeing isn’t just a PR-friendly marketing record — it’s proof that battery swaps work. And, when you see how simple it is to add hundreds of miles of driving in under two minutes (quicker, in many cases, than pumping a tank of liquid fuel into an ICE-powered car), you might come around.

title: Brazil’s retail electricity market opening raises credit and liquidity concerns, study finds - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A study based on 88,000 consumer units participating in subscription-based solar generation schemes in Brazil has identified a 17% average monthly payment delinquency rate and 4% monthly customer churn. The findings highlight potential credit, liquidity and consumer protection challenges as the country prepares to open its free electricity market to low-voltage consumers.
Alessandra Neris
10 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Brazil’s planned opening of its free electricity market to low-voltage consumers could require stronger credit assessment, liquidity management, regulatory oversight and consumer protection mechanisms, according to a study by energy market specialists Guilherme Susteras and Alexandre Bueno.
The study draws on a Wattio database covering 88,000 consumer units linked to 1,400 shared solar plants across the service areas of 40 electricity distributors between January 2025 and May 2026.
The researchers found an average monthly payment delinquency rate of 17% and monthly customer churn of 4%, potentially resulting in turnover equivalent to more than 40% of the customer base over a year.
The findings provide a reference point for assessing risks that could become more pronounced as Brazil expands access to its free electricity market.
Under the planned regulatory timetable, industrial and commercial consumers will be able to migrate to the free market from Nov. 25, 2027. Other consumers, including residential customers, will become eligible from Nov. 25, 2028.
Credit and liquidity risks
The researchers said the expansion of the retail electricity market will require regulatory oversight to extend beyond monitoring the physical and energy balance of the system.
“It will not be enough to monitor only the system’s physical and energy balance. Issues such as working capital, liquidity, contractual robustness, credit assessment, anti-fraud mechanisms and commercial practices will become increasingly important for the sustainability of the retail market,” said Susteras.
The study found that a fragmented customer base does not eliminate payment delinquency risks. In a highly competitive market, significant levels of overdue payments could put pressure on electricity retailers’ cash flow and undermine their ability to meet financial obligations.
The researchers called for stronger credit assessment, guarantee and receivables management mechanisms from the initial stages of market expansion.
Pricing pressure
Competition for customers presents another potential challenge. The study found that subscription-based solar generation offered an average annual discount of 17%, rising to 19% in 2026.
The researchers warned that customer acquisition costs, payment delinquency, working capital requirements and competitive pressure could encourage electricity retailers to reduce margins excessively in pursuit of market share.
“In a market with significant customer acquisition costs, payment delinquency and working capital requirements, a strategy based exclusively on lower prices can jeopardize the financial sustainability of operations,” said Susteras.
He added that retailer bankruptcies could leave consumers dependent on a supplier of last resort, potentially exposing them to higher electricity prices.
Customer churn and oversupply
The study also identified monthly customer churn of 4% as a source of pressure on operating costs.
Contracts with limited exit barriers, poor customer understanding of energy products, aggressive sales practices and price competition all contribute to customer turnover, according to the researchers.
Another concern is unused project capacity, which occurs when shared solar generation projects fail to attract enough subscribers to absorb their available output.
The researchers said investments made before sufficient demand materializes could increase financial exposure for market participants.
A similar situation could emerge in the free electricity market if excessive contracting increases retailers’ exposure to Brazil’s short-term electricity market, particularly if contracted supply grows faster than customer demand.
Information asymmetry
The researchers also highlighted the challenges of serving smaller electricity consumers.
Citing data from Brazilian restaurant and bar association Abrasel, the study noted that energy is not among the main priorities of small business owners, who tend to focus on staffing, supplies, sales, marketing, taxation and administrative requirements.
As a result, some consumers may enter into electricity supply contracts without fully understanding their commercial terms, billing arrangements or contractual obligations.
“Information asymmetry is a critical issue. Situations arise in which consumers claim not to recognize contracts or have difficulty understanding the charges shown on their bills,” said Bueno.
Contracting timelines could further complicate the customer experience.
In subscription-based distributed generation, the period between signing a contract and receiving the associated benefits can extend to 90 days. A similar period may apply between cancellation and a return to previous supply arrangements.
According to the study, the start of supply by a retailer in the free market could involve a comparable timeframe, while returning to the distribution utility could take up to a year.
For consumers unfamiliar with electricity supply contracts, these delays could increase uncertainty and perceived risk.
Broader regulatory oversight
Opening the market to low-voltage consumers is also expected to increase operational complexity because of differences in metering and billing procedures among Brazilian electricity distributors.
The researchers said problems affecting customer experience could become indicators of regulatory stress as the number of retailers, consumers and contractual relationships increases.
“The ability to oversee contracts and commercial practices, combat fraud, monitor liquidity and payment delinquency indicators, and manage different metering and billing processes will be decisive in establishing a broader and more sustainable market,” said Susteras.
The study was developed by Allez Estratégia, a consultancy specializing in energy regulation and retail electricity markets. It draws on the experience of Susteras and Bueno, who led Brazilian solar company Sun Mobi from 2016 to 2025.
The researchers cautioned that the experience of subscription-based distributed generation does not necessarily predict how the free electricity market will develop. However, they said it provides indicators of risks that could become more significant as retail competition expands.
They concluded that market liberalization will require not only greater consumer choice but also stronger governance, regulatory frameworks and risk management practices.

title: Austria: 43,300 applications for solar subsidies submitted in just ten minutes - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Austria’s final solar subsidy round of the year attracted 43,300 applications in its first 10 minutes, far exceeding demand in the previous round. The government is now preparing to overhaul the scheme in 2027, shifting its focus from PV installations to battery storage and smart energy management systems.
Sandra Enkhardt
10 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Residential
Austria opened its third and final funding round of the year for photovoltaic systems and battery storage on Thursday afternoon. Demand was even higher than in the previous round, according to an announcement issued Friday by the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs, Energy and Tourism.
Preliminary figures show that around 43,300 application tickets were issued within 10 minutes of the opening of the Renewable Energy Expansion Act (EAG) funding portal, operated by funding agency OeMAG. By comparison, the second funding round in the summer attracted 24,900 tickets in its first 10 minutes.
The ministry said it had anticipated strong demand based on previous funding rounds. The experience has also prompted the government to reconsider its approach to PV subsidies.
Earlier this week, the ministry presented initial proposals for a revised funding scheme following extensive consultations with representatives of the electrical engineering industry, electrical retailers and industry association PV&B Austria.
“We need to move away from a race against the clock and toward a subsidy system that allows individuals and businesses to plan effectively,” said Elisabeth Zehetner, Austria’s state secretary for energy.
Smart energy management to become mandatory
Under the proposed scheme, applicants would be able to submit funding requests together with their final invoices after completing their projects, starting in 2027.
Applications would be accepted year-round, replacing the current system of three annual funding windows in which applicants compete to secure funding on a first-come, first-served basis.
The ministry also plans to replace conventional investment grants with a battery storage bonus. The new scheme would prioritize battery storage systems installed alongside new or existing PV arrays, provided they are connected to a smart energy management system.
Such systems would be mandatory to qualify for funding.
The ministry is still finalizing the details, including the storage bonus amount and technical eligibility requirements. It said the necessary legislative amendments are being prepared.
The changes would require a two-thirds majority in parliament, meaning the governing parties would need support from the opposition.
Austria introduced its current system of multiple annual funding rounds in 2021. Although the scheme has supported PV deployment, the ministry said it no longer meets market requirements.
It also pointed to organized efforts to improve applicants’ chances of securing funding, including dedicated training sessions and online courses.
“It is absurd that specific training courses and organized voucher campaigns are being set up just to access a subsidy,” Zehetner said. “This illustrates the grotesque extremes to which this subsidy logic has led. That is precisely why we are changing the rules of the game: subsidies must facilitate investment rather than turning into a race to see who can click the fastest.”
European-made inverters to be required for new installations
The proposed overhaul aims to give households and installers greater planning certainty while simplifying the application process. The government also wants the scheme to support European manufacturing.
“A ‘Made in Europe’ inverter will be mandatory for storage systems installed alongside new PV systems. An additional ‘Made in Europe’ bonus for storage systems retrofitted to existing PV systems will remain available,” the ministry said.
The proposed changes could also benefit applicants who missed out on funding this year.
According to the ministry, PV systems equipped with smart battery storage that are invoiced or commissioned on or after Nov. 1, 2026, would be eligible to apply for funding under the new scheme in 2027.
Industry calls for clarity on funding rules
Herbert Paierl, CEO of PV&B Austria, welcomed the increased emphasis on battery storage but called for greater flexibility in the proposed European-content requirements.
“We welcome the fact that battery storage is becoming a greater focus of subsidy schemes,” Paierl said.
“Regarding the ‘Made in Europe’ requirement, we see room for a broader and more practical approach. The foundation has been laid. Now, the details must be shaped in a way that ensures planning certainty for businesses, allowing them to know well in advance what framework conditions will apply in 2027.”

title: Sunbooster secures European patent for bifacial photovoltaic fences - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Austrian company Sunbooster has secured a European patent for its bifacial solar fence technology, now protected in 18 EU member states. The company is expanding into France, where it has completed its first 3.7 kW installation using vertically mounted PV strips with a reported efficiency of 22.8%.
Gwénaëlle Deboutte
10 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Residential
Austrian company
Sunbooster
has secured a European patent for its vertical photovoltaic solution designed for integration into fences.
The technology is now protected in 18 European Union member states, and the company aims to expand its presence in the French market.
Sunbooster’s solution consists of 18.6 cm-high bifacial PV strips that slide into existing fence panels, replacing conventional privacy slats. Each strip has a rated output of 62 W for a 2-meter length or 79 W for a 2.5-meter length, with a reported conversion efficiency of 22.8%. The vertical orientation is designed to shift a portion of electricity generation toward the morning and late afternoon hours.
“We are expanding our presence, particularly in France, where we have already completed our first installation,” Yann Schremmer, Sunbooster’s France manager, told
pv magazine
. The company has installed a 20-meter section of solar fencing in Aix-en-Provence, with a total capacity of 3.7 kW. The system was supplied by a metalworking company and integrated into the fence of a customer seeking both privacy and electricity generation.
The 2-meter strip is priced at €619 ($692.9( for residential customers, while the 2.5-meter version costs €719. “We have deliberately set very attractive prices for professionals, allowing them to achieve high margins,” said Schremmer. The company plans to focus on building a distribution network comprising PV distributors, major retailers, and fence manufacturers.
The bifacial PV strips use p-type monocrystalline solar cells cut into quarters. Designed for rigid double-wire mesh fences (6/5/6 mm or 8/6/8 mm), the strips are inserted into the mesh and connected using MC4 connectors located on the bottom strip.
According to the manufacturer, the strips have an IP67 protection rating and an operating temperature range of −20 C to 60 C. The maximum system voltage is 50.16 V for the 2-meter version and 63.84 V for the 2.5-meter version.

title: Why leadership decides Italy's energy security - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
At Solar & Storage Live Italia, panels organised by Women in Solar+ Europe (WiSEu) and Solar+ Leaders argued that decisions made in a project’s first months, and the inclusive teams built to make them, matter as much to energy security as megawatts and capital.
Women in Solar+ Europe
10 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Solar plants are built to run for 30 years or more, yet the choices that shape those decades are often made in a matter of weeks, under pressure to hit pipeline targets. A panel organized by the Solar+ Leaders ecosystem at Solar & Storage Live Italia asked what it takes to lead with that long horizon in mind, arguing that resilience and energy security depend as much on the people who lead the sector as on the capacity they deploy.
Early decisions, long consequences
A recurring theme was that much of a solar plant’s fate is sealed at the start. Letizia Petracci, Vice President Technical at Starlight Energy, part of the NextEnergy Group, pointed to Italy’s connection queue: requests for renewables exceed 300 GW, roughly four times the new capacity foreseen in the national plan to 2030. Since September, grid access goes to whoever obtains authorization first, not whoever applies first, which raises the stakes on choosing which projects to pursue.
Why does that choice weigh so heavily? Because, as Petracci explained, the developer is the first link in the chain: its decisions are inherited by those who build, finance and operate a plant for 30 years, and by the community that hosts it. In its first weeks, a project is cheap and still easy to stop; the further it advances, the harder it becomes to say no, not for technical reasons, but because pipeline targets loom and the time already invested feels wasted. The new rules sharpen the dilemma: developers must now move fast and carry projects all the way to authorization with no certainty of a connection.
“Leadership is measured above all in a little-celebrated skill: knowing how to decide early, and honestly, what not to do,” Petracci said. Speed built on competence and organization pays off, she argued; haste simply passes the cost of shortcuts to whoever comes next.
David Moser, managing director Italy at Becquerel Institute, spent 13 years leading a research group at Eurac in Bolzano studying how PV plants age and degrade. He has repeatedly seen plants underperform after eight or ten years because of choices made by people who have since moved on. “Whoever takes shortcuts isn’t getting ahead: they are offloading a cost onto someone else in the value chain, and sooner or later that cost comes back,” he said. Now developing AI tools for PV, Moser warned that fast answers can become a shortcut to not thinking, and that tools must show what they are based on and where they are uncertain, so that a person can still take responsibility for the decision. Now more than ever we need to develop and apply critical thinking.
Holistic thinking, connected teams
Domenico Biasi, government and regulatory affairs at Sonnedix, framed renewable plants as long-term assets that stay in a territory for decades. An IPP, he said, must be recognized not only as able to build, but as a serious investor that keeps its commitments, which means weighing financial, social, environmental and regulatory risks together. “Responsible leadership does not give up on performance; it makes it sustainable,” Biasi said, calling for cross-functional teams involved from day one and T-shaped professionals who combine deep expertise with the ability to talk across disciplines.
For Maria Sabella, founder and CEO of Enlight Energy Services, which supports investors across the lifecycle of Italian utility-scale PV, continuity is the overlooked risk. Plants often change hands, so service providers must preserve their operational memory. “Our leadership is key to maximizing team retention and encouraging continuous training, so that knowledge is not concentrated but shared and preserved,” she said. Sabella also stressed long-term partnerships and genuine value co-creation with key suppliers, and the growing need to connect plant owners with energy consumers whose core business lies elsewhere.
Projects that keep working
Angelica Almi, head of legal at ESCo Kataclima and co-founder of Italia Rinnovabile, a benefit cooperative developing renewable energy communities, warned against mistaking compliance for impact. “One of the most dangerous temptations is confusing a project that ‘works’ with a project that ‘will work’,” she said. A community can meet every deadline and secure its incentives, yet fail if governance is unclear or citizens don’t understand how benefits are shared. Almi also urged organizations to give young professionals responsibility before they have 20 years of experience – otherwise, she noted, companies end up searching for talent someone else has trained.
Moderating the panel, Gulnara Abdullina, Advisory Board Member at Circular Synergies, the organisation behind Solar+ Leaders, commented: “I opened by asking whether our leadership models are evolving as fast as the energy systems we’re building. Our panellists, Maria, Letizia, Domenico, Angelica and David, shared their very diverse experiences and identified the typical risks associated with weak leadership. None of these risks was capacity or technical problems. They are judgment calls, made by usually one person, usually early, before there’s any data to back the decision up. That’s what “intelligence in leadership” actually means in this sector: not having the answers, but building an inclusive organisation that lets someone make the call and be backed for making it.”
The people-centred theme carried into an additional session organised by Women in Solar+ Europe (WiSEu) where speakers argued that teams that flag a weak project early and share knowledge rather than hoard it, depend on something more basic: environments where everyone feels safe to speak, and is expected to.
Maribel Otaño, Country Manager Italy at Solis: “I witnessed something fundamental when it comes to psychological safety: creating spaces where people feel safe to share their opinions is not a luxury. It’s essential. At Solis, my team and I work every day to foster an environment where all voices are truly heard. For me, it’s critical that the decisions we make are based on active listening, without judgment, without dismissal, always with respect. When that happens, people speak up early. They challenge ideas. They contribute what they really think. And the quality of what we build improves. This responsibility is not just mine as a leader. It belongs to everyone in the organization. Each person decides, every day, whether to create that safety and protect it. That takes commitment from leadership and courage from everyone else, and it’s worth the investment.”
Elena Maspoli, founder of Greenspire, has followed renewables from the finance side as they grew from a pioneering niche into a sector employing nearly 2 million people in the EU. As the industry matures, she noted, skills become more specialised and organisations more complex, requiring constant dialogue between project management, legal, external relations and structured finance. Inclusive organisations are also a retention tool, as candidates increasingly weigh work-life balance alongside role and pay.
Maspoli described psychological safety as something built through small “nudges”, borrowing Nobel laureate Richard Thaler’s term. A manager who asks the team for ideas before imposing a decision, and explains why ideas are set aside, teaches people to form and share opinions. The main obstacle, she said, is often time, in organisations focused on getting results as fast as possible. “In the long run, what creates a stable organisation is getting from A to B with the contribution of everyone involved,” Maspoli said. For those without formal authority, her advice was to occupy spaces rather than wait for them: a silence or hesitation in a meeting can be the moment to put forward a solution.
Ercilia Estrada, project manager oversight at Gruppo Undo, an integrated industrial operator and IPP with around 150 MW installed, pointed to trust and mutual respect, recognition of everyone’s contribution and a culture of candid, constructive feedback. But she stressed that safety brings responsibility. “When everyone knows they can speak up, it becomes essential to also take responsibility for putting one’s skills at the service of the organisation,” Estrada said, calling for a solution-oriented mindset rather than simply describing problems. She applied the same logic to battery storage: developing BESS in Italy involves institutions and private operators alike, and will depend on leadership that strengthens coordinated collaboration among all of them every day.
Diversity as a source of resilience
Giulia Muia, an independent advisor who connects foreign investors and IPPs with developers, EPC contractors and landowners, and who helps energy-intensive clients through the energy transition, brought the view of someone who has often been both the youngest and the only foreigner in the room, after a decade in Germany working in M&A, strategy consulting, investment funds and IPPs. A classicist by training, she started from etymology: security comes from the Latin sine cura, “without worry”, meaning, at work, without fear of being judged too harshly for speaking up or making a mistake. That matters most when you are young. She recalled how, as a junior strategy consultant, the head of her company would sit down with her, open his notebook and ask how things could improve, writing down her answers. “He probably knew it all already, but in that moment I felt I could tip the scales,” she said. “That confidence taught me to take space, and later to give it.”
Being a foreigner, she added, raises the bar further. In meetings in Germany, she had the ideas but had to express them in a language learned at 20. “Speaking on the street is one thing; speaking in a meeting is another. I needed more time to say the same things.” That kind of space rarely appears on its own; it has to be deliberately created. For Muia, everyone has to be heard: the young, women, foreigners, and those who lack the expected title or credentials. Their input should then be integrated and judged on its merits. Her example came from the field: engineers and geologists can complete every study, yet it is the local farmer who warns that the land floods. “The information that changes a project often comes from the source you least expect,” Muia said. Just as no one would build energy security on a single source, she argued, diversification is what makes teams resilient. But that space cannot depend on the courage of the youngest or the most exposed: empowerment has to come top-down, not bottom-up. With the sector expanding fast, now is the time to train and integrate new talent: “We have a rare chance to build an industry’s culture as it is born, instead of having to correct it later.”
Across both sessions, the common thread was clear: Italy’s energy security will depend not on the megawatts requested, but on the megawatts actually built, connected and operated well for decades, and on leaders, with or without a formal title, who create the conditions for every voice to shape the choices that get them there.

title: More than 70% of announced U.S. solar manufacturing expansion plans yet to be financed - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Forecasted capital expenditure for new U.S. solar manufacturing expansions for 2027 reflects a hesitant financing climate, with Tesla’s Texas plans having the potential to rocket boost the entire sector’s spending outlook.
Finlay Colville
10 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Manufacturing
Solar Manufacturing USA
In the final part of the special Austin-debrief series of articles this week in
pv magazine
, I review the outlook for U.S. solar manufacturing capital expenditure (capex) by quarter to the end of 2027.
For reference, Part 1 of the series addressed
domestic U.S. module production forecasting
, capturing themes covered at the recent
Solar Manufacturing USA 2026
event in Austin, Texas on 22-23 September, with Part 2 looking at
cell production by quarter to the end of 2027
The analysis underpinning the data and conclusions within each of the articles is taken directly from the new
Solar Manufacturing USA Quarterly
The bottom-up analysis from more than 50 companies in the U.S. manufacturing space for 2027 shows that solar PV manufacturing capex is forecast to see a year-on-year decline compared to the final numbers expected for 2026 (circa. $3 billion).
U.S. solar manufacturing capex peaked in 2024 (almost $4 billion), with more than half this spending coming from just two companies; First Solar and Qcells.
The forecast for 2027 solar manufacturing capex reveals that more than 70% of the announcements made by companies over the past 12-18 months (that would have necessitated spending in 2027) are either unfunded or stranded.
Waiting in the wings however is potentially the most disruptive play ever to be seen in the history of U.S. solar PV manufacturing; Tesla’s mega-sized ingot-to-module manufacturing plans.
It is getting close to factoring in Tesla’s manufacturing capex plans to the analysis that forms the basis of the new
Solar Manufacturing USA Quarterly
report and indeed using the capex phasing to drive the incremental production volumes across the silicon-based value-chain in the United States.
This would appear to be the missing link in forming a credible 2030 capex and production forecast – something that the downstream buying community and the upstream equipment/materials supply side is badly in need of. Many have spent the past few years looking at interactive pins-on-maps, a trend that was started back in 2022 by U.S. trade associations and government-based portals (once the IRA was introduced) and has no shortage of variants these days.
The financing details and phasing of solar manufacturing capital expenditure ultimately hold the key to forecasting domestic U.S. productivity out to 2030 and beyond. I will return to 2030 production forecasting in the coming days, pending the ‘Tesla’ question.
Why is solar manufacturing capex forecast to decline in 2027?
Those who heard my talk at the recent
Solar Manufacturing USA 2026
event in Austin, Texas on 22-23 September will recall me stating that capex is the most important aspect of solar market research and part of understanding this relates to spending cycles.
End-markets can grow during capex downturns, but a capex downturn is likely a symptom of other industry factors that could have longer-term implications.
Figure 1 Excluding Tesla and other upside PV manufacturing capex in 2027, investments in domestic U.S. PV manufacturing are still adapting to the initial post-IRA flurry that was loaded into 2024 as First Solar and Qcells committed record levels of capex to the U.S. sector.
Since 2025, solar manufacturing capex in the United States has been going through a minor downturn cycle. This is a consequence of two factors.
First, the capex by First Solar and Qcells, that was loaded mostly into 2024, was significant in comparison to the overall spending trends of the 20-30 companies that were investing in the U.S. manufacturing space at this point. The loading into 2024 can therefore be regarded as a one-time hit, or an annual outlier. Had the spending phases from either or both companies been spread more into 2023 or 2025, the peak seen in Figure 1 for 2024 would not have been so pronounced.
Second, outside the capex from First Solar and Qcells, there is no other ‘major spender’ at the billion-dollar annual level. Therefore, although the number of manufacturing sites associated with solar manufacturing capex in the United States in the past few years now exceeds 60, the total capex figures for 2025, 2026 and 2027 are all well below the peak seen in 2024.
But the big issue for 2027 is not the specific capex number being forecast. It is driven by Tesla. When will spending start for real? How long does the company plan to keep Chinese equipment in warehouses?
No longer ‘if’, the changes are coming soon. Forecasting U.S. solar capex and production is set to move into unchartered territory

title: Beyond gigawatts: Why India’s clean energy future depends on storage intelligence - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The battery creates flexibility. The intelligence behind it determines how much of that flexibility the grid can harness. The next clean energy benchmark for India, therefore, might not just be a new number of gigawatts. It might be the ability to get the maximum out of every gigawatt.
Kumar M., founder of Smart Grid Analytics
10 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Grid integration
Highlights
Utility-scale
Kumar M., founder of Smart Grid Analytics
For decades, the success of India’s renewable energy transition has largely been measured in gigawatts. That indicator remains relevant, but it is no longer sufficient. The more important question today is how effectively the electricity system can accommodate, coordinate, and derive value from the renewable capacity being added.
The scale is significant. As of Sept. 30, 2026 data, India had 299 GW of renewable energy generation capacity, including 171 GW from solar and 59 GW wind. Total non-fossil capacity stood at 308 GW, according to the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE). These numbers demonstrate the scale India has achieved. They also point to the operational challenge ahead.
Solar and wind cannot provide electricity on demand. Solar generation peaks during the day while electricity consumption can remain high in the evening. Wind generation varies with weather conditions and location. As variable renewable energy grows, the challenge is no longer only about expanding generation. It is about coordinating generation with consumption and making the power system increasingly responsive.
This challenge will become even more pronounced. The International Energy Agency sees India’s electricity demand increasing at an annual rate of 6.4% up to 2030, adding more than 570 TWh to annual electricity consumption. The agency also sees variable renewable energy accounting for 24% of India’s electricity generation in 2030, compared with 14% in 2025.
With demand growing alongside variable generation, flexibility becomes an imperative for India’s power grid, not just an option.
This is where Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) become critical. Yet conversations around BESS often begin and end with capacity. While capacity matters, it is far from the sole determinant of system value.
Consider a battery supporting a solar plant. Charging whenever excess solar is available may appear sensible. But what if a demand surge is anticipated later? What if the battery needs to maintain a minimum state of charge for ancillary services? What if committed schedules, market opportunities, or grid requirements change during the same operating period? What if aggressive cycling creates value today but reduces the battery’s useful life?
The value of storage therefore depends not only on how much energy a battery can store, but on the continuous decisions made around that stored energy.
This is where storage becomes an intelligence problem.
The magnitude of the requirement is evident in India’s planning documents. According to the Central Electricity Authority (CEA), integrating 364 GW of solar and 121 GW of wind up to 2031-32 would require 73.93 GW/411.4 GWh of energy storage capacity. Of this, 47.24 GW/236.22 GWh would be BESS. As per end-of-2024 figures, India’s energy storage capacity stood at just 4.86 GW, of which 0.11 GW was BESS.
This shifts the purpose of the Energy Management System
An EMS can no longer be treated merely as a tool for monitoring assets or following pre-programmed schedules. In a renewable dominated environment, it has to become the decision-making system connecting generation, storage and grid requirements.
This requires bringing together multiple real time inputs: forecasted generation, demand, state of charge, committed schedules, grid conditions, deviation risk, market signals, charging and discharging limitations, and battery degradation.
The objective is not simply to ensure that the battery is charged and ready. It is to continuously determine when that stored energy will be most valuable and how it should be deployed without compromising technical, operational, or economic requirements.
In other words, the system must be able to sense, predict, decide, and execute.
That intelligence cannot exist through EMS alone. As renewable plants become more complex, SCADA, Power Plant Controllers, forecasting, optimisation and Energy Management Systems increasingly need to operate as parts of a coordinated control architecture.
A renewable or hybrid plant may contain multiple assets and systems, but the grid ultimately needs the plant to behave as one coordinated, predictable, and responsive entity.
That requires reliable visibility into what is happening, the ability to anticipate what is likely to happen, intelligence to determine the appropriate response and control systems capable of executing it.
The February 2025 Advisory issued by the CEA demonstrates this change in system requirements. It recognised the significance of storage for grid stability, reliability and effective utilisation of energy and recommended that future solar tenders include at least two hours of storage located alongside the solar farm, equal to 10% of solar capacity.
This takes the conversation beyond batteries and into the technology that manages and coordinates them.
India’s cleantech opportunity, therefore, is not only about the mass production of solar panels, wind turbines and batteries. It is also about building the intelligence and control systems required to make these components work together.
Indigenous EMS, SCADA, PPC, forecasting and optimisation systems can acquire strategic significance as the grid becomes increasingly dynamic and storage assets are expected to perform multiple functions.
At Smart Grid Analytics, this is how we have approached the renewable energy control problem: not as a collection of isolated software systems, but as an intelligence layer connecting renewable generation, storage and the grid.
The underlying requirement is straightforward. The system needs to know what is happening across the plant, anticipate changing conditions, decide what should happen next, and translate that decision into coordinated action.
This becomes increasingly important as the number of assets, operating conditions, and decisions increases. Monitoring alone is no longer enough. A dashboard may show the state of charge, generation or grid condition, but creating value requires determining what action should follow from that information.
The opportunity for India is therefore larger than developing indigenous individual technologies. It is to build indigenous expertise in making sense of an increasingly complex flow of data about generation, storage and grid conditions, and turning that data into coordinated decisions.
This also indicates that the next wave of energy metrics needs to go beyond installed capacity numbers.
Gigawatts and gigawatt hours will continue to be important indicators of physical size, but they should increasingly be supplemented by utilisation, responsiveness, renewable energy accommodation, availability, provision of grid services and the value created from installed capacity.
India has proven that it can create renewable capacity at large volumes. The challenge ahead is determining whether that capacity can become increasingly responsive, coordinated, and efficient.
The next phase of the energy transition will therefore require more than generation and storage assets. It will require the intelligence layer that connects them.
The battery creates flexibility. The intelligence behind it determines how much of that flexibility the grid can harness.
The next clean energy benchmark for India, therefore, might not just be a new number of gigawatts.
It might be the ability to get the maximum out of every gigawatt.

title: The shape of PPAs is changing – from volume to value - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Australia’s renewable energy market is entering a new phase where the value of electricity is increasingly determined not by energy alone, but by the ability to deliver energy when and where it is needed.
Anita Stadler, Giles Walgenwitz, Martin Bates
10 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
in early 2025 that the energy transition was overlooking a critical market: the market for risk. Eighteen months after, and the shift from simply paying for renewable output to demanding firmness and shape is already evident. An example deal being the 600 MW, 12-year South Australian (SA) supply
agreement
between Firmus and Swiss commodity trading firm Gunvor.
As coal-fired power stations retire, they remove not only physical generation capacity from the National Electricity Market (NEM) but also a significant source of financial hedging products. This will increasingly impact market liquidity of traditional ASX and Over the Counter (OTC) hedging products and drive demand for a new generation of bulk renewable energy, shaping and firming services.
Large renewable energy generators and battery owner-operators can no longer stand on the sideline.
The intersecting policy catalysts, redefining revenue strategies over the next 3-to 5-years
Several intersecting policy initiatives have been driving the transition to a renewable power system in the NEM, with the Federal Capacity Investment Scheme (CIS) taking over from the Commonwealth Renewable Energy Target (RET) Scheme to incentivise pre-2030 investment in renewables and storage alongside the New South Wales (NSW) Long-term energy services agreements (LTESA), Victorian Renewable Energy Target (VRET) Scheme and SA Firm Energy Reliability Mechanism (FERM).
Australia’s renewable energy market is now approaching a significant inflection point. Looking beyond 2030, the Electricity Services Entry Mechanism (ESEM) proposed by the
NEM Wholesale Market Settings Review
Panel, is expected to become a key driver of long-term investment in renewables and storage.
Importantly, the ESEM is emerging at the same time as Federal and state government policy initiatives. These policies place obligations on data centres to contract for new renewable supply, as well as address shaping and firmness to contribute towards system reliability.
These policy developments respond to the same underlying market reality: buyers will be seeking solutions that combine energy, shape and firmness. ESEM attempts to create liquid products for these services, while emerging data centre policies seek to mandate their procurement. Together they signal a fundamental shift away from energy-only PPAs.
Unlocking the value premium: why ESEM and data centres are reshaping renewable offtakes
Several intersecting policy initiatives have been driving the transition to a renewable power system in the NEM, with the Federal Capacity Investment Scheme (CIS) taking over from the Commonwealth Renewable Energy Target (RET) Scheme to incentivise pre-2030 investment in renewables and storage alongside the NSW Long-term energy services agreements (LTESA), Victorian Renewable Energy Target (VRET) Scheme and SA Firm Energy Reliability Mechanism (FERM).
Australia’s renewable energy market is now approaching a significant inflection point. Looking beyond 2030, the Electricity Services Entry Mechanism (ESEM) proposed by the
NEM Wholesale Market Settings Review
Panel, is expected to become a key driver of long-term investment in renewables and storage. Importantly, the ESEM is emerging at the same time as Federal and state government policy initiatives. These policies place obligations on data centres to contract for new renewable supply, as well as address shaping and firmness to contribute towards system reliability.
These policy developments respond to the same underlying market reality: buyers will be seeking solutions that combine energy, shape and firmness. ESEM attempts to create liquid products for these services, while emerging data centre policies seek to mandate their procurement. Together they signal a fundamental shift away from energy-only PPAs.
Unlocking the value premium: why ESEM and data centres are reshaping renewable offtakes
Unlike earlier support schemes, the ESEM is intended to create liquid, standardised products capable of bridging the gap between short-dated exchange-traded contracts and the long-term revenue certainty required to finance large renewable and storage projects.
To achieve this, products must be sufficiently fungible and detached from the characteristics of individual projects to support secondary market trading. This represents a fundamental departure from the traditional run-of-plant PPA model.
The legislation and rules required to implement the first tranche of priority ESEM products are expected to be finalised by
March 2027
. Based on the current design, key implications for renewable generators and storage owners are significant.
Rather than transferring shape and volume risk to buyers, sellers will increasingly be expected to manage and underwrite these risks themselves. Capturing the value premium and tenure available under the ESEM will favour asset operators with diversified portfolios, sophisticated trading capability and an ability to manage shape, volume and firmness risk over long contracting horizons.
At the same time, data centres are rapidly emerging as a new category of buyer. The AEMC’s
to the Commonwealth, the
NSW Data Centre Guidelines
Victorian Sustainable Data Centre Action Plan
point towards future obligations that require large data centres to support additional renewable generation, firming capacity and demand flexibility. Unlike the corporate PPA buyers that dominated the first wave of renewable procurement, data centres may need integrated solutions that address renewable energy, firming and compliance requirements simultaneously.
Practical implications of fungibility?
This simply means one MW or MWh is interchangeable with another identical unit, regardless of which project underpins the product. Products must thus be standardised to ensure liquidity. This implies a shift away from the physical project context that has driven many key commercial terms (e.g. force majeure, thermal curtailment, etc.) under run of plant, tolling and capacity swap agreements.
For sellers, data centres represent a substantial growth opportunity. However, the capabilities required to compete effectively in this market are likely to mirror those needed under emerging ESEM product constructs, namely the ability to package energy, shaping and firmness solutions through sophisticated portfolio and risk management.
Monitor data centre policy evolution and potential tension at state and federal levels
This is early days in shaping data centre policies, with significant work still to be done to align federal and state policies. To prepare your organisation to be well positioned to capture the data centre opportunity, you must carefully consider both the similarities and differences between the obligations proposed at Federal and state level.
Whilst the Victorian energy- related recommendations for data centres suggest alignment with the Commonwealth framework, subject to finalisation, the NSW Government’s proposals differ from the AEMC’s recommendations in several material respects, as outlined below.
Looking ahead: the next generation of offtake markets
Data centres represent an attractive new class of renewable energy buyer. They have large and growing electricity demand. Furthermore, unlike many energy-intensive industrial sectors, electricity costs, while significant in absolute terms for data centres, often represent a smaller proportion of overall operating costs, which combined with emerging renewable energy and firming obligations may increase both their willingness and ability to pay for renewable energy and firming services.
Whilst significant uncertainty remains around both data centre policy settings and the implementation of NEM Review and ESEM reforms, it is increasingly clear is that the market is moving beyond traditional run-of-plant PPAs. The retirement of coal generation, the emergence of ESEM, and the rapid growth of data centres are accelerating the unbundling of value into three distinct categories:
Bulk renewable energy
Shaping services
Firming services
In this environment, future buyers are likely to seek integrated solutions that combine these elements within a single offtake arrangement. The organisations best positioned to succeed in this next phase of the energy transition are therefore unlikely to be those with the lowest-cost wind, solar or battery assets alone. Instead, competitive advantage will increasingly reside with participants that can offer:
Structure products that solve buyer obligations rather than simply sell electricity
Effectively monetise shaping and firmness alongside energy, backed by sophisticated trading and risk management capabilities
Operate diversified renewable and storage portfolios.
Does your organisation have the trading, portfolio and risk-management capabilities needed to compete in this future market?

content:
Markets & Policy
Australia has endorsed a global plan to double the number of homes in the world with rooftop solar, from 150 to 300 million by 2030 via the Global Rooftop Solar Declaration announced at the 2026 Pacific Pre-COP meeting in Fiji.
Ev Foley
10 Oct 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Australia is the first country to endorse a global plan to double the number of homes with
rooftop solar
Global Rooftop Solar Declaration
at the 2026 Pacific Pre-COP meeting in Fiji.
The Declaration is a roadmap for governments to make residential solar and battery systems easier and cheaper to install by cutting red tape, offering affordable finance, upgrading power grids and training local workers.
The Declaration underpins the 300 Million Solar Homes initiative, and its partners – including the Global Solar Council, Smart Energy Council (SEC) Australia and Solar Citizens – welcomed Australia’s endorsement and called on other governments at a national, regional and local level to follow.
Minister Bowen endorsed the Global Rooftop Solar Declaration at the 2026 Pacific Pre-COP31 meeting in Fiji, 8 October 2026
Image: Australian Government
Minister for Climate Change and Energy and President of Negotiations for COP31 Chris Bowen announced in Fiji the launch of the Global Rooftop Solar pledge.
“Australia has 35% of their houses with rooftop solar. We’re working to spread rooftop solar more around the world,” Bowen said.
SEC Australia Chief Executive Officer David McElrea the Australian government has shown it is prepared to take Australia’s global rooftop solar leadership to the world.
“Rooftop solar cuts power bills, gives countries greater control over their own energy and protects households and economies from volatile fuel costs and supply,” McElrea said.
Solar Citizens Chief Executive Officer Heidi Lee Douglas rooftop and home solar is the
sleeping giant
in global climate diplomacy, despite powering millions of homes.
“This pivotal Declaration provides a pathway to rapidly change that. We now call on national, state and local leaders around the world to sign onto the Global Rooftop Solar Declaration ahead of COP31 and help bring the benefits of home solar to millions more people,” Douglas said.
Global Solar Council Chief Executive Officer Sonia Dunlop added that it took the world around 30 years to reach the first 150 million solar homes.
“We want to add the next 150 million in just four years. Australia’s support and practical experience in implementation is exactly what we need to realise that ambition in every corner of the world,” Dunlop said.
Global Rooftop Solar Declaration
Signatories will support practical collaboration on city, state and regional delivery partnerships, rooftop solar
policy design
, finance models for households, grid integration and storage, consumer protection and safety, training and workforce standards, data and deployment tracking, and access models for low-income and underserved communities.
Rooftop solar, and battery storage, is one of the fastest-growing parts of the global energy system, expected to deliver 42% of solar growth and 34% of all renewable energy growth by 2030.
