title: Can Beijing end the race to the bottom? - pv magazine Global
content: China’s solar industry has spent two decades proving how far costs can fall. It is now confronting a harder question: how low is too low? The need for an answer has become urgent. In the first half of 2026, some of China’s largest solar manufacturers remained deeply in the red despite technological gains and enormous shipment volumes. Tongwei posted a net loss of CNY 5.12 billion ($763 million), Longi CNY 3.68 billion, TCL Zhonghuan CNY 3.20 billion, JinkoSolar CNY 3.08 billion and JA Solar CNY 2.66 billion. Together, the five companies lost more than CNY 17 billion in six months. The industry has been exceptionally good at adding capacity, but far less effective at removing it. Persistent oversupply has pushed prices below levels that support normal returns, while companies have kept factories running to preserve cash flow, employment and market share. “Production capacity across all segments of the PV supply chain has exceeded demand projections for 2035. Capacity clearance remains the industry’s greatest challenge,” noted BloombergNEF PV analyst Tan Youru. Beijing has stepped up its response. What began as appeals for industry self-discipline has evolved into a broader “anti-involution” campaign – which has become a common Chinese policy term for curbing excessive, self-defeating competition, especially repeated capacity expansion and price-cutting that destroy returns across an entire industry. In solar, that campaign now combines price regulation, standardized cost accounting, mandatory efficiency and energy-consumption rules, tax changes and pressure for capacity rationalization. The objective is not simply to lift module or polysilicon component prices, but rather to terminate the incentives that allowed destructive competition to persist. Hard constraints China’s latest solar downturn is unusual because losses alone have failed to clear the market. Solar manufacturing is capital intensive. Once a factory is built, a producer may keep operating at poor margins as long as sales contribute toward fixed costs. Large manufacturers are reluctant to cut first if it means competitors would gain market share. Local governments, lenders and suppliers also have motivations to keep plants alive because closures affect employment, tax revenue and debt repayment. Technology transitions further complicate this scenario. Older capacity does not disappear when a new generation of equipment is installed. It is preferred to remain in the market at lower prices to maximize its value, while its owner invests in newer lines to avoid falling behind. This results in a prolonged adjustment rather than a clean correction. Since the fourth quarter of 2024, China’s PV industry has endured a sustained price decline lasting more than 20 months, with corporate operating profits collapsing in tandem. That’s why policy is shifting to include enforceable constraints. Standardized accounting One potentially decisive change came in July, when the China Photovoltaic Industry Association (CPIA) released a standardized cost-accounting model covering the main links of the PV manufacturing chain. What does selling “below cost” mean? For years, the industry has lacked an answer. A manufacturer can cite cash cost, manufacturing cost or full cost. Integrated producers can allocate costs differently from specialized producers. Depreciation, financing expenses and related-party transactions can materially alter the result. “Cost advantage has always been one of China’s core competitive strengths in solar,” said CPIA Executive Secretary-General Liu Yiyang. “But if prices remain detached from companies’ true costs for too long, reasonable investment and sustainable operations cannot be guaranteed.” The cost model combines voluntary reporting and sample audits, according to CPIA. Member companies submit monthly production-cost data for each manufacturing segment, which are aggregated and anonymized to calibrate the model. Since the second quarter of 2026, Deloitte and EY have conducted sample checks on participating companies, examining raw-material procurement prices, depreciation policies, related-party transactions and whether losses are being shifted outside the reporting entity. Audit results are graded and unreliable data are removed from the model’s sample pool. CPIA also uses cross-checks to validate submissions. Yan Dazhou, director of the National Engineering Research Center for Silicon-Based Materials Preparation, said the standard ends a situation in which “everyone defines costs differently” and provides a practical benchmark for enforcing rules against below-cost bidding. That framework was tested almost immediately. On Aug. 6, eight major polysilicon producers, accounting for more than 90% of China’s effective polysilicon capacity, signed an anti-involution pledge committing to keeping sales prices, including tender bids, at or above the corresponding full cost calculated in the CPIA model. At the end of July, average dense polysilicon prices were around CNY 31.5/kg. Industry estimates put full cost broadly at CNY 40/kg to 50/kg. Prices then moved sharply higher. InfoLink’s Sept. 9 assessment put mono-grade polysilicon at CNY 38/kg to 43/kg, averaging CNY 40/kg. Two days later, commodities data provider Mysteel estimated n-type polysilicon at CNY 40.5/kg, against production cost of CNY 42.3/kg and full cost of CNY 45.6/kg. The gap has narrowed, but average prices remain below estimated full cost. Nor has the underlying imbalance disappeared. InfoLink said actual transactions remained scattered, with large downstream buyers reluctant to accept higher prices, while September polysilicon output was expected to rise and inventories continued to build. So far, anti-involution has changed price expectations faster than supply-demand fundamentals. Survival thresholds Price discipline is only one part of the reset. China has issued three mandatory national standards covering energy consumption in polysilicon and monocrystalline silicon production and efficiency requirements for crystalline-silicon modules and inverters. All three take effect on Jan. 1, 2027. Existing polysilicon plants using the dominant trichlorosilane process must keep comprehensive energy consumption at or below 6.3 kg of standard coal equivalent per kilogram of polysilicon. For modules, the minimum Grade 3 conversion-efficiency threshold is 23.2% for tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) and heterojunction (HJT) products and 23.5% for back-contact (BC). These are legal thresholds. Plants or products that cannot comply must be upgraded or removed from the market. The potential impact of the new thresholds is substantial. The Silicon Industry Branch of the China Nonferrous Metals Industry Association estimates that China’s effective polysilicon capacity will fall to around 2.4 million metric tons (MT) annually after restructuring. That would be 16.4% below the level at the end of 2024 and 31.4% below roughly 3.5 million MT of installed facilities – implying about 1.1 million MT of nameplate capacity being cleared. Some market analysts expect an even larger impact downstream. CITIC Securities said in an Aug. 22 report that the efficiency thresholds could cut around 45% of outdated cell capacity, reducing n-type cell capacity from 1 TW to about 600 GW. Huatai Securities estimates that up to 327.6 GW of module capacity, or 33% of the total, could be eliminated. Even under its most conservative scenario, in which every manufacturer upgrades existing lines to the best technically achievable level, it still sees 153.6 GW, or about 15%, permanently leaving the market. But the headline figures overstate the likely short-term impact if they count capacity that is already offline. CITIC Futures Research argues that much of the polysilicon capacity failing the new standards is already idle “zombie capacity” – unprofitable, debt-ridden manufacturing output. Removing this may slash nominal capacity statistics while barely changing actual supply. Significant shift There are signs of real change. Executives at several polysilicon producers told pv magazine that roughly 1.1 million MT of nameplate capacity across second- and third-tier companies is currently shut and has no restart plan. Qinghai Lihao has permanently closed 80,000 MT of older, high-energy-consumption capacity. Asia Silicon’s production lines are largely shut, while capacity at producers including Qiya Group, Ginno, Goens, CSG, Dun’an, Hongyuan Green Energy, Huamin and smaller producers in Yunnan, Hubei and Gansu is broadly idle, according to executives interviewed. Still, idled is not the same as permanently removed. Much of that capacity has not been physically dismantled and could be returned if economics improve. But doing so would require its owners to bear substantial restart costs. Downstream companies are showing restraint by canceling expansion before it is built. Aiko has terminated a planned 15 GW TOPCon cell project and is instead converting existing capacity toward its all back-contact (ABC) technology. Trinasolar has abandoned the 15 GW second phase of a planned 35 GW monocrystalline ingot project after completing the first 20 GW. Industry executives told pv magazine that Longi, JinkoSolar and JA Solar have also largely frozen capacity-related capital expenditure. A senior executive at one leading manufacturer said Jan. 1, 2027, will be the decisive test. Once the mandatory standards take effect, operating lines that fail Grade 3 requirements will face a legal choice between upgrading or closing. Permanent exit, the executive said, will then move from canceling planned projects to retiring or dismantling existing operating capacity. That is the real test, as higher prices alone do not equal restructuring. If prices recover and idled factories simply restart, or companies launch another expansion cycle, anti-involution will have only postponed the problem rather than solved it. The indicators that matter are capacity utilization, inventories, permanent closures, mergers and acquisitions, operating cash flow, gross margins, capital expenditure and new capacity announcements. “The sustained push against ‘involutionary’ competition will drive profound changes in the industry’s competitive landscape,” said Wang Jian, an analyst at TrendForce Consulting. He said he expects market share to concentrate among companies with stronger technology, cash flow and global reach, while manufacturers dependent on simple capacity expansion and lacking technological upgrade capabilities will exit faster. In that sense, anti-involution is already becoming a consolidation policy, even if it is not formally described as such. Future stability For global buyers, a successful reset would probably mean a firmer floor under Chinese module prices. That may marginally raise procurement costs, but it could also reduce the risks of financially weak suppliers, aggressive cost cutting and long-term warranty exposure. China is changing what its manufacturers are rewarded for. Scale, cost and market share remain important, but efficiency, energy use, product quality, financial resilience and technological differentiation are gaining weight. Fiscal policy reinforces that change. VAT export rebates have been removed, while conventional solar cells will face a 2% consumption tax from April 2027, rising to 4% a year later. Perovskite, tandem and gallium-arsenide cells remain exempt through 2028. The direction is clear. Policy is becoming less supportive of simply producing more mature products, and more selective about technology and efficiency. But the reset will only succeed if capacity actually leaves the market. China has proved it can make solar extraordinarily cheap. The next test is whether it can make the industry financially sustainable without surrendering the cost and technology advantages that made it dominant. title: Scientists achieve 13-qubit genuine entanglement without destroying their photons
content: Quantum computers may one day tackle problems that overwhelm conventional machines, but getting enough quantum bits to work together remains a major challenge. Now, in a new study, a team of Chinese researchers has demonstrated a way to join smaller groups of entangled microwave photons into larger, programmable quantum networks without destroying the photons during the connection process. They showed genuine entanglement across 13 photonic qubits, offering a potential route toward more scalable quantum computing and communication systems. The challenge lies in making these connections reliably. Quantum bits, or qubits, can be linked through entanglement, a quantum phenomenon in which their shared state cannot be described independently. Scientists can arrange these connections into structures called graph states, which act as resources for quantum computing and communication. “Large photonic graph states are important resources for quantum communication, quantum networks and measurement-based quantum computing,” Hongyi Zhang, senior study author and a quantum researcher at Tsinghua University, told Phys.org . One way to link smaller entangled states is through a process called fusion, which joins them to form a larger state. However, conventional fusion methods used in linear-optical systems often work probabilistically, meaning some attempts fail. Repeated attempts and additional hardware can make building larger states increasingly demanding. The trick to joining photons without destroying them The study authors introduced a strategy that uses a superconducting circuit to join smaller entangled groups of microwave photons. Rather than creating one enormous entangled state in a single process, the approach builds a larger network by connecting smaller, prepared states. The key to this approach is a technique called quantum nondemolition measurement. Unlike a measurement that absorbs or destroys the photons, this method can extract information while preserving the photons themselves. In this experiment, the measurement also transforms the pair’s joint quantum state, allowing the researchers to connect smaller graph states. “We asked whether fusion could instead be made deterministic by using a quantum non-demolition measurement. Our goal was to demonstrate a deterministic, programmable fusion operation and show that it can provide a practical route to assembling larger, reconfigurable photonic graph states.” Zhang said. How the researchers connect the photons The researchers first generated small, entangled groups of microwave photons using the superconducting circuits. They encoded quantum information in different time slots of the photons, allowing information to be carried in distinct arrival times. They then used the quantum nondemolition detector to measure selected photon pairs and project them into a specific entangled state called a Bell state. This allows the smaller graph states to be joined without destroying the photons. Next, by adjusting the photons’ frequencies (also called frequency tuning), the researchers can select which pairs undergo the measurement, controlling how smaller graph states connect to form a larger one. This makes the fusion process programmable. The team also incorporated active resetting and reuse of superconducting qubits, along with built-in error mitigation, to help limit the effects of decoherence , the loss of delicate quantum properties through interactions with the environment. Using this method, the researchers demonstrated genuine multipartite entanglement across 13 photonic qubits. This means the entanglement extended across the entire group rather than being limited to isolated, smaller groups. This achievement demonstrates that the fusion process can produce larger, reconfigurable photonic graph states. “Our main contribution is a fusion operation that is deterministic, programmable and nondestructive,” Zhang said. A step toward scalable quantum networks Large photonic graph states could support measurement-based quantum computing, in which computations are performed through carefully chosen measurements on an entangled state. They could also help advance quantum networks and quantum error-correction schemes, which aim to protect quantum information from errors. “The work offers an architecture for scaling photonic graph states by connecting smaller, on-demand resource states. This is relevant to future measurement-based quantum computing, quantum networking and potentially quantum error-correction schemes, where both the size and the connectivity of graph states matter,” Zhang explained. However, demonstrating entanglement across 13 qubits is not the same as building a practical, large-scale quantum computer. The system still needs improvements in the accuracy of the device, photon-generation efficiency, and detector performance. Therefore, the researchers now plan to develop multiple-detector architectures that can perform more fusion operations and generate larger, more complex graph states. Whether this approach can scale efficiently while maintaining the required performance remains to be seen. The study is published in the journal Nature Physics .

title: US firm aims to speed 390 MW nuclear reactor deployment with phased build plan
content: Terrestrial Energy has submitted its Thermal and Electric Facility (TEF) Topical Report to the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC). The filing proposes a bifurcated regulatory model that could allow key non-nuclear components of its power plant to be built and operated prior to receiving a full nuclear license. If accepted, this strategy would resolve one of the atomic sector’s steepest economic hurdles. Traditional atomic projects often face extensive delays because safety reviews generally encompass both the reactor and its major steam-generating systems. Under this new pathway, only the nuclear module follows the exhaustive atomic licensing schedule, while the turbine complex proceeds under standard commercial timelines. To roll out commercial units The regulatory gambit comes as major institutional energy consumers seek dependable, round-the-clock clean power. The US Army’s Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland is reportedly set to host a 390-megawatt-electric (MWe) IMSR plant. The installation at the military’s oldest active test base would help shield critical defense operations from wider grid failures. To roll out these commercial units quickly during the 2030s, the developer relies on an architectural divide. The design physically splits the site into two distinct zones. The primary module contains the nuclear core. A separate auxiliary building houses standard energy equipment, such as steam systems, heat exchangers, and electrical turbines. Terrestrial Energy wants federal regulators to formally confirm that assembling this turbine wing falls outside federal nuclear construction rules. That administrative distinction carries immediate financial benefits. Erecting the non-nuclear wing under commercial industrial building codes allows developers to offer lenders predictable timetables and lower capital risks. Operators could customize the power block for local industrial demands before nuclear fuel arrives. Sites could even fire the turbines using natural gas as a temporary heat source. This bridge would generate revenue while reactor permits finish their regulatory run. Independence from power-conversion systems Safety remains the decisive factor for federal overseers. Terrestrial Energy’s technical filing demonstrates that the core nuclear module operates with complete independence from the power-conversion systems. Relying on accident assessment methods that the NRC has already approved, the company proved that an equipment breakdown within the turbine building cannot spread into the nuclear core. The filing represents Terrestrial Energy’s third formal submission delivered to federal regulators this year. The agency has already approved the company’s baseline design standards alongside its core safety criteria. Separate technical submission A separate technical submission covering the qualification of reactor-grade graphite is currently under review. Once ratified, these findings create permanent licensing precedents. They eliminate repetitive technical evaluations for subsequent commercial builds. “Approved Topical Reports establish foundational elements of the IMSR licensing basis that may be referenced in future applications without re-evaluation, reducing the scope of subsequent technical review,” noted Terrestrial Energy. Unlike conventional high-pressure light water reactors, the IMSR runs at atmospheric pressure and extreme heat using standard-assay low-enriched uranium fuel. “The IMSR Plant is small, modular and designed to supply low-cost, reliable, high-temperature heat and electricity for industrial applications, including data centers, and chemical and petrochemical supply,” concluded the company.

title: Vision-based waste-sorting robot identifies high-value recyclables in real time
content: Scotland-based Danu Robotics has just received $5 million in seed funding for its novel waste sorting robot called “H.E.R.O.” Designed to autonomously identify and sort recyclable materials, systems like this promise to make recycling more profitable and efficient. At present, when you drop something into a recycling bin, that doesn’t necessarily mean it is destined to actually be recycled. The first hurdle is whether it actually gets to a recycling plant, as, all too often, recycling waste may just be combined with regular waste streams. But, assuming it does, the recycling plant then has several issues to overcome. The first is potential contamination. Recyclable bulk waste is often mixed, combining plastics, paper, food waste, and other materials. To be efficiently recycled, these materials need to be sorted, cleaned (where applicable), and concentrated. Recycling needs a H.E.R.O. This is often carried out by trained human workers on a conveyor belt, which is not only time-consuming but also prone to error. Especially as human workers tend to get tired and bored quickly. Robots, like Danu’s H.E.R.O. , on the other hand, don’t get tired and could, in theory, work continuously. To achieve this, Danu’s robot employs a mixture of cameras, AI, and robotic arms to identify and sort waste much like a human would. The cameras act as its eyes, able to continuously feed its onboard AI with visual data of what items are on the conveyor belt. The AI then identifies and classifies waste by its “recycling worth.” This refers to the fact that not all materials can be economically viable to recycle, so spending energy and time to recover them is often a losing game. Once identified, the AI then instructs the robot’s grippers to grab the item from the waste stream, ready for processing. Grippers are important here as they are able to manipulate heavier and more awkward items when compared to other options like suction cups. The latter can struggle here, so grippers are the more effective method in Danu’s view. This could help improve the bottom line for recycling facilities significantly, according to Danu Robotics. They believe a facility using these systems could easily improve revenue by at least $485,000. Sorting at source Given that the robot itself costs about $160,000 in initial investment with around $24,000 in ongoing maintenance costs, that’s quite a healthy return on investment. And the market appears to be taking notice. Beyond the seed funding, the company has announced that it has received at least 2 letters of intent to buy and has around $500,000 in signed contracts. It also has about 200 potential customers in its sales pipeline, not bad for a company founded only 6 years ago. There aren’t confirmed sales as yet, but it shows that there is a potentially very strong demand for it once mature enough for release. Looking ahead, Danu also sees potential for its robot technology to be deployed in many other places, not just recycling centers. Once miniaturized enough, it could, for example, be deployed in places like shopping centers, airports, or office buildings. “Once it’s smaller, it can be used as a stand-alone recycling solution for events, for shopping centers, hospitals, or airports to recycle their waste at the source,” Danu Robotics founder Amy Ma told TechCrunch . “And that’s the way we can really change how we’re managing our packaging waste,” he added.

title: Heavy cargo drones airlift 143-pound loads to North Sea wind turbines
content: Ørsted reports that it has completed a new trial of a large cargo delivery drone at its North Sea Hornsea 2 offshore wind farm. According to the company, the trial was to test whether drones could be a viable way to replace routine sea vessel trips for maintenance operations and costs.The trial was run in conjunction with Skyports Drone Services (Skyports) using one of its large cargo drones. According to a press release, the Skyports team developed a novel load-collection method with automatic hook operation for the trial.Importantly, the drones were operated beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS), meaning drone operators didn’t need to keep visual contact with the drones. In this case, the team demonstrated delivery across roughly 2.5 miles (4 km) of the wind farm without even seeing them. This, the team explained, reduced human involvement as much as possible by allowing the drone to pick up and drop off payloads all by itself. The trial ran for around four weeks and required collaboration from a diverse team of safety, aviation, drone operators, and other technicians. Ørsted used drones to do the dog workIt also required close coordination with the United Kingdom’s Civil Aviation Authority. As for the kits, each weighed between 121 pounds (55 kg) and 143 pounds (65 kg) and contained tools, spare parts, and other materials for specific tasks.These packs were then delivered to different turbines before technicians arrived to carry out work. After completion, drones were then used to collect the used kits and return them to the Service Operations Vessel (SOV).Impressive, but what is the need? Well, traditionally, maintenance kits of this nature tend to be shipped to site. Once there, the kits need to be hoisted up to the wind turbine, which is both time-consuming and potentially dangerous.Drones, on the other hand, can deliver packages from point A (the SOV) to the work site (the top of the turbine, say) with relative ease. It also opens the door for the possibility of emergency part delivery on site with little to no delay.“The offshore environment is a challenging one – traditional turbine logistics, either through vessels or helicopters, involve time, coordination, varying levels of risk and cost. At Hornsea 2, we’ve shown the potential for cargo drones as a viable alternative that minimizes these factors,” Skyports Drone Services CEO Alex Brown said in a press release.Cheaper and safer than ships“These drones give wind farm operators like Ørsted a practical way to reduce lifting and vessel movements, get technicians working faster and maximize the time turbines spend generating,” he added.It is important to note that this isn’t the first time Ørsted has experimented with heavy-lift drones at its offshore wind farms. But this latest trial is the first to feature more automated cargo pickup and return, as well as proving its utility under real conditions. “This trial confirms our approach to integrating drone-enabled maintenance into our routine operations. By delivering parts and tools more efficiently and safely, we can improve turbine uptime and reduce emissions and operating costs,” Richard McCrilley, Project Lead at Ørsted, explained. “As we had a daily presence, we were able to cater for a variety of ad-hoc flight requests and get equipment sent out to support the teams. We were able to cover both planned and reactive works,” he added.

title: Pentagon expands quantum computing push to secure military tech edge
content: The Pentagon is committing around $350 million to advance US quantum computing capabilities, as Washington seeks to turn emerging research into technologies with potential military applications, including more efficient logistics, advanced materials development, and next-generation weapons systems.The initiative is part of a broader push to maintain US leadership in a field that could eventually transform encryption, materials science, logistics, and weapons development.The investment comes as both the US and China expand their quantum research programs. While practical, large-scale quantum computing remains a major engineering challenge, governments are increasingly treating the technology as a strategic capability rather than just a scientific pursuit.Strengthening military capabilities through quantum computingThe US Department of War announced the initiative through the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, which advises the Pentagon on emerging technologies. “Dominance in quantum information science is a critical priority for both President Trump and the Department of War. Maintaining American leadership in this field is essential to preserving our technological edge, and R&E is uniquely positioned to drive the innovation needed across academia and industry,” Emil Michael, Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering, said in a statement.The initiative follows a June executive order aimed at accelerating quantum technology deployment, commercialization and domestic manufacturing. The Pentagon expects the resulting capabilities to support the development of next-generation weapons, platforms and other military systems that could be more effective, affordable and easier to manufacture.Quantum computers process information using quantum-mechanical effects, allowing them to tackle certain problems differently from conventional computers. Their potential applications include modeling advanced materials and chemical reactions, optimizing complex logistics networks and addressing some computational problems that are impractical for today’s systems.Cryptography is another area of strategic interest, since sufficiently powerful quantum computers in the future could break widely used public-key encryption methods, although today’s machines cannot yet do this at the scale required. That prospect has also accelerated efforts to develop quantum-resistant cryptography.US, China expanding their quantum programsChina has made quantum technology a strategic research priority, backed by substantial state investment. The country established its National Laboratory for Quantum Information Sciences in 2017, and its 2026–2030 five-year plan identifies quantum research and applications as areas of focus.Chinese military interest extends to potential cyberwarfare applications. A 2026 report described more than 10 experimental quantum cyberwarfare tools as being under development by the People’s Liberation Army. Their capabilities and operational maturity, however, remain unclear.Washington is also responding with funding across defense and civilian research programs, as US lawmakers have reportedly discussed increasing annual military spending on quantum development and applications by 68%, to $567 million, according to Bloomberg. The US Department of Energy has also launched the Quantum Genesis Q Competition, offering up to $215 million to companies working toward fault-tolerant quantum computers.The Pentagon’s latest initiative comes alongside additional support for companies attempting to build useful quantum computers, the South China Morning Post reported. Its Office of Strategic Capital has signed a conditional loan commitment worth $150 million with PsiQuantum, and the funding is intended to strengthen the company’s advanced manufacturing and prototyping capabilities in the US.

title: US Army links electronic warfare systems to counter enemy signals
content: The US Army has demonstrated how three electronic warfare and cyber technologies can work together to identify hostile communications and disrupt them using software-driven radio-frequency effects, potentially shortening the time needed to counter adversary signals on the battlefield.The demonstration, led by the Army’s Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Command, Control, Communications, Computers, Cyber, Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance Center (C5ISR Center), took place at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, from August 5 to 8. Soldiers from the 11th Cyber Battalion participated in the exercise, which connected three previously separate programs for the first time.The integrated system combines the Tactical Development Kit (TDK), Tactical Radio Frequency Application Chassis (TRAC), and Warped Alloy software. Together, they are designed to detect signals, analyze their characteristics, and generate electronic effects to interfere with adversary communications.Three systems work as oneEach component has a distinct role in the process. TRAC is a ruggedized, open-architecture platform that monitors the electromagnetic spectrum, supports mission planning, and delivers non-kinetic electronic effects. It is built around the Army’s Cyber/EW, Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance Modular Open Suite of Standards (CMOSS), which supports modular integration of capabilities.When TRAC detects a signal of interest, it can pass the information to TDK. The system contains a forward-deployed library of known adversary signals, based partly on the US Cyber Command Arsenal’s list of signals of interest. It also uses artificial intelligence and machine learning to help analyze unfamiliar signals and identify their frequencies and waveforms.That information can then inform a response through Warped Alloy, a software framework that generates radio-frequency effects at the communications-protocol level. According to the Army, this approach differs from older electronic warfare methods that primarily attempt to overpower hostile communications with electromagnetic energy. Instead, Warped Alloy is designed to interfere with the protocols governing how communications systems operate.Adapting to changing enemy signalsDuring the demonstration, the Army simulated a battlefield scenario in which hostile forces communicated while preparing an attack. TRAC detected the signal and passed relevant data to TDK for analysis. The resulting information was then used to determine a Warped Alloy response, delivered through a software-defined radio hosted by TRAC.The Army says Warped Alloy can dynamically reconfigure compatible tactical software-defined radios to maintain communications denial as adversaries switch between primary, alternate, contingency, and emergency communications channels.The system is designed to continue denying communications until the underlying protocol changes, at which point the signal-identification and response process can begin again.The goal is to reduce the time between detecting a transmission and delivering an appropriate electronic countermeasure. Rather than relying entirely on fixed capabilities or lengthy development cycles when new threats emerge, the Army wants to develop modular effects that can be adapted to changing requirements.However, the August event was a demonstration of the systems’ integration, not evidence that a finished, fully automated battlefield capability is ready for deployment.Toward a common electronic warfare frameworkArmy officials described the demonstration as a step toward a “develop once, deploy everywhere” framework for non-kinetic cyber and electromagnetic effects. The idea is to develop reusable software capabilities that can operate across compatible hardware platforms, reducing the need to build a separate solution for every new threat.The Army released the underlying Warped Alloy software framework to industry in January to encourage developers to integrate it into different software-defined radio architectures. Data collected during the demonstration will inform further development. Planned work includes additional exercises with soldiers, improvements to usability, and integration into a single interface so operators do not have to move between separate computers to manage the process.For the Army, the objective is to give cyber warfare units more adaptable tools for operating in contested electromagnetic environments, where adversaries can change their communications methods to evade detection and disruption. The demonstration showed how spectrum monitoring, AI-assisted signal analysis, and software-based electronic effects could be integrated into a coordinated workflow. However, further testing and refinement are needed before the planned integrated system is complete.

title: World’s first ammonia powered bulk carrier enters service for Australian iron ore
content: A 300-meter bulk carrier capable of running on ammonia is entering service to transport Australian iron ore. It marks a milestone for Belgium-based CMB. TECH’s nearly decade-long effort to develop large ships that run on the alternative marine fuel.The 210,000-dwt Mineral Europa is embarking on its maiden voyage to Australia. Chartered to Fortescue, it is set to carry iron ore from Western Australia’s Pilbara region to China and other international markets.The vessel forms part of CMB. TECH’s broader push to decarbonize shipping, with a fleet of 21 ammonia-powered vessels targeted by the end of 2029.CEO Alexander Saverys described the ships as the beginning of the “propulsion revolution” and said Mineral Europa “proves that large ocean-going ships can be powered by ammonia.”Dual-fuel engine and deck-mounted tanksBuilt by CSSC Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding Co., Mineral Europa uses a dual-fuel engine that can run on ammonia or conventional marine fuel. The engine was developed through a partnership with WinGD.The ship has a reported speed of 14 knots. It is owned by Bocimar, CMB.TECH’s dry bulk shipping business, and is managed by Anglo-Eastern.According to CMB.TECH, liquid ammonia is stored in independent tanks positioned on deck, at a safe distance from the vessel’s sides. The company has established safety protocols, and every crew member must complete training before boarding.CMB.TECH said the vessel would operate on “green ammonia,” produced using renewable power, water, and air. However, it did not address the fuel’s current availability for its vessels.The company also said it is developing the fuel ecosystem needed to support the transition to cleaner shipping.Fortescue charter covers 12 bulk carriersMineral Europa joins Mineral Latvia, with both vessels registered in Belgium.In June 2026, CMB.TECH announced that Fortescue would charter 12 Newcastlemax bulk carriers. Up to three were scheduled to enter service in 2026 with dual-fuel ammonia engines.The remaining nine were designated ammonia-ready, meaning they could be converted to operate on the fuel. A separate agreement announced in March 2025 involves Japan’s Mitsui O.S.K. Lines and MOL Chemical Tankers.Under that arrangement, MOL and CMB.TECH jointly own three 210,000-dwt Newcastlemax vessels being built at Qingdao Beihai Shipyard. Deliveries are scheduled for 2026 and 2027, with the ships operating under 12-year charters to MOL.CMB.TECH is also building two ammonia-fitted and four ammonia-ready chemical tankers at China Merchants Jinling Shipyard in Yangzhou.These vessels are scheduled to join the fleet in 2028 and 2029 under seven- to 10-year charters with MOL Chemical Tankers.Ammonia fleet remains smallBy the end of 2029, CMB.TECH plans to have 18 dry bulk vessels, one containership, and two chemical tankers powered by ammonia.The expansion comes as ammonia propulsion remains in its early stages.DNV’s cited data listed five ammonia-fueled vessels in service: two gas carriers, two tugboats, and Fortescue’s demonstration offshore support vessel.Four dry bulk carriers, including CMB.TECH vessels, were undergoing testing. Another 41 ammonia-fueled ships were on order for delivery by 2030, indicating a growing pipeline for a fuel still represented by only a handful of operating vessels.

title: Giant tortoise count hits 183,000 on Seychelles island, study shows
content: As many as 183,000 giant tortoises thrive in the Seychelles, a new survey has found. The Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea) are said to be an endangered species. A survey led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter found that the identified population is the “highest figure ever recorded for the species.” The discovery is a huge victory for conservation efforts across the Indian Ocean.Population rise The current population contrasts sharply with the late 19th century, when hunting and habitat exploitation nearly drove the reptiles to extinction. It left fewer than 1,000 survivors on the isolated coral ring. Swift intervention reversed their decline after Aldabra was designated a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1982. Rigorous legal protection combined with the successful eradication of invasive feral goats in 2012 ultimately paved the way for this historic recovery.“The monitoring data in this study were collected by SIF staff living and working on the atoll, year after year. More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra,” said Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of SIF. A baseline for the futureHowever, determining the population count was not straightforward. It required almost five years of dedicated field monitoring by SIF researchers alongside statistical experts at the University of Exeter. The actual counting process proved to be a complex challenge.Aldabra’s landscape consists of sharp coral and thick, tangled vegetation. Tortoises routinely seek shade under dense bushes, vanish into mangroves, or shelter from the scorching equatorial sun. Previous surveys relied on raw headcounts. As a result, older estimates, such as the long-cited 100,000 figure from the late 1990s, likely missed tens of thousands of hidden animals.To fix this, researchers used Bayesian hierarchical distance sampling. It is an advanced statistical method that models missing data. The technique mathematically corrects for unseen reptiles across different habitats, from open “tortoise turf” grasslands to impenetrable scrubland. Rather than a sudden surge, the new estimate shows the population has always been strong, thriving, and secure.Despite the encouraging news, scientists stress that caution remains essential as the island’s fragile ecosystem faces serious environmental threats. Rising sea levels risk submerging low-lying habitats, and increasingly severe droughts threaten to dry up food and shade. Also, invasive rats and cats continue to prey on vulnerable tortoise eggs and hatchlings. Together, these threats underscore the need for ongoing protective measures.“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.Plans to eradicate the remaining invasive mammals is already underway. But for meantime, Aldabra Atoll offers a rare story of hope, showing a landscape where nature rebounded from near collapse and giant tortoises reclaimed their habitat.The study findings were published in the journal Ecology and Evolution

title: 2,800-lb unmanned vehicle with higher payload to showcase firepower
content: A new type of unmanned ground vehicle with higher payload capacity is set to showcase its battlefield power. The Hunter WOLF multi-mission unmanned ground vehicle has been selected to advance to Phase II of the GroundBreaker 1 unmanned ground vehicle demonstration. The Hunter WOLF is a multi-mission unmanned ground vehicle engineered to reduce soldier workload, extend operational reach and keep personnel farther from dangerous tasks. Its adaptable architecture supports missions including tactical logistics, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, casualty evacuation, communications support and other mission-critical applications.Mature, and mission-ready platform“Hunter WOLF was built for exactly this kind of challenge,” said Tom Van Doren, President, Robotics Sector at BLADE. “This is a mature, mission-ready platform that has been tested alongside warfighters in demanding environments. GroundBreaker 1 gives us the opportunity to demonstrate why the Hunter WOLF is ready to support the warfighter now.”GroundBreaker 1 is designed to evaluate unmanned ground vehicle technologies for potential employment across tactical and non-tactical missions. During Phase II, Government evaluators will assess technology maturity, operational readiness and cross-domain interoperability.BLADE announced that HDT Robotics, LLC, doing business as BLADE, has been selected to advance to Phase II of the GroundBreaker 1 unmanned ground vehicle demonstration with its Hunter WOLF multi-mission unmanned ground vehicle.Hunter WOLF combines high payload capacity, off-road mobilityDesigned for complex and austere environments, Hunter WOLF combines high payload capacity, off-road mobility, onboard power, autonomous and remote-control capabilities. The system has been evaluated through military exercises and training events and has supported operational use in Ukraine, providing BLADE with real-world insight into evolving unmanned ground requirements, according to a press release.The GroundBreaker 1 selection comes as the Department of War places increasing emphasis on rapidly fielding autonomous and robotic systems capable of operating alongside warfighters. Following Phase II, companies whose demonstrations are successfully evaluated may be invited to Phase III to submit a full proposal for a Prototype Other Transaction Authority award, as per the release.The Hunter WOLF is designed to support a broad range of military missions through an adaptable, multi-mission architecture. Its intended applications include tactical logistics, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), casualty evacuation (CASEVAC), communications support, and other mission-critical operations.By transporting supplies, supporting reconnaissance activities, and assisting with casualty evacuation, unmanned ground vehicles can potentially reduce soldiers’ physical workload while extending their operational reach. Their ability to perform selected tasks remotely may also help keep personnel farther away from dangerous situations.BLADE’s selection for Phase II highlights the continuing development of unmanned ground systems designed to support military operations in demanding environments. With its multi-mission configuration and experience in military exercises and operational settings, Hunter WOLF will now face a further assessment of its capabilities at Camp Grafton.

title: New smartwatch tracks sodium, potassium in 165-minute field test
content: Researchers in Japan have developed a wristwatch-type sensor that tracked sweat-related sodium and potassium signals for 2 hours and 45 minutes during a real-world construction site test.The wearable device, developed at Tokyo University of Science, combines printedelectrodes, a sweat collection layer and wireless electronics to monitor changes in sweat chemistry while a person works.Unlike conventional printed sensors that can require lengthy preparation before producing stable readings, the new system uses a liquid-junction reference electrode designed to stabilize quickly.The prototype was tested on one construction worker during normal activities, including movement, breaks, drinking water and eating. Researchers say the results demonstrate that the system can collect and transmit sweat-related signals outside laboratory conditions.Printed electrodes speed stabilizationThe sensor measures changes in electrical voltage associated with sodium and potassium ions in sweat. These minerals are involved in several physiological processes, making them useful targets for wearable monitoring research.Such sensors rely on a reference electrode to provide a stable electrical baseline. Without it, changes in voltage cannot be reliably linked to changes in ion concentration.Conventional printed reference electrodes can take considerable time to stabilize, limiting their usefulness in wearable systems designed for continuous measurements.To address this, the researchers integrated a screen-printed liquid-junction reference electrode containing silica gel. The material allows water to enter the electrolyte layer, helping the electrode reach a stable measurement potential without lengthy pre-adjustment.The device also includes separate sodium- and potassium-selective electrodes, allowing it to respond to both ions.A layer of fabric and superabsorbent fiber sits above the electrodes. It helps collect sweat, keep the sensing area wet and transport samples across the sensor.The components connect to a custom wristwatch-type electronic unit that processes the signals, transmits them wirelessly to a computer and stores the measurements on a microSD card.The researchers say the combination of these components, rather than the development of a new electrode material, is the main engineering advance.Construction site trial succeedsThe team tested the complete system at an active construction site, where a worker wore the device for approximately 165 minutes while performing normal daily activities.During the trial, the sensor continuously acquired signals responsive to sodium and potassium. The readings were transmitted to a nearby computer and saved locally.“The central achievement of this work lies not in the proposal of a new electrode material, but in the integration of a printed electrode, sample transport mechanism, and wireless measurement circuit, demonstrating its feasibility in a real-world environment,” said Isao Shitanda, an associate professor at Tokyo University of Science who led the research.The field test involved only one participant. Researchers also emphasized that the signals have not yet been validated as accurate quantitative measurements of sweat electrolyte concentrations under controlled sweating conditions.Further testing will be needed before the device can reliably support hydration assessment or health monitoring.The team believes printed electrode manufacturing could eventually make similar wearable systems inexpensive to produce at scale.Potential applications include monitoring workers at construction sites and factories, as well as athletes and people exercising outdoors in hot conditions.The study was published in ACS Omega.

title: China's Starlink links Arctic and Antarctic in satellite video call
content: China has demonstrated a new capability for its Guowang satellite network, connecting researchers in the Arctic with personnel in Antarctica through a video call with less than one second of reported delay. The test offers an early glimpse of Beijing’s efforts to build an independent satellite communications system that could eventually rival SpaceX’s Starlink.State broadcaster CCTV reported the call in late September. Researchers aboard three Chinese polar expedition vessels connected with personnel at the country’s Qinling Station in Antarctica. The experiment also tested data transfers between research ships and China’s National Marine Data and Information Service.Guowang remains far smaller than Starlink, but Beijing sees independent satellite connectivity as strategically important. The network could support communications across remote regions where conventional infrastructure struggles to reach.China builds its satellite networkChina Satellite Network Group, a state-owned operator, manages the Guowang constellation. Satellite launches began in December 2024, and just over 180 spacecraft have entered orbit so far. The company ultimately plans to deploy 12,992 satellites by 2035.The current network still faces significant limitations in coverage and overall data capacity. China aims to place 400 satellites in orbit by the end of 2027, providing coverage across the country. Its longer-term target calls for approximately 1,300 satellites by late 2029.The polar experiment also tested whether Guowang could transmit practical operational information. Researchers exchanged data files and voyage logs with a Chinese marine information agency. These capabilities could help expedition teams coordinate activities across isolated waters without relying on foreign communications providers.CCTV described the experiment as progress toward independently controlled polar communications. Keeping sensitive information within China’s own infrastructure also aligns with Beijing’s concerns about data security.Starlink still holds a leadThe researchers recorded peak upload and download speeds of approximately 30 megabits per second. That performance could support video calls and many routine data transfers, although actual speeds depend on network conditions.SpaceX’s Starlink generally offers download speeds between 25 and 220 Mbps, depending on location and service conditions. Its much larger constellation also gives the US system a substantial advantage in coverage and capacity.Starlink operates roughly 11,000 satellites, compared with Guowang’s current fleet of just over 180. That gap matters beyond consumer internet access. A larger network can provide more opportunities to maintain connections as satellites move across the sky, although performance also depends on network architecture and ground infrastructure.Chinese military observers have suggested that a 30 Mbps connection could support tactical communications and potentially enable real-time control of uncrewed systems. However, bandwidth alone does not establish a satellite network’s military effectiveness. Resistance to electronic jamming, network resilience, and dependable coverage also matter.Starlink’s role in supporting Ukrainian communications during Russia’s full-scale invasion has helped demonstrate the strategic value of low-Earth-orbit satellite networks. China has restricted foreign satellite communications services within its territory, citing data security concerns.Another Chinese constellation emergesGuowang is not China’s only major effort to expand satellite connectivity. Shanghai Spacesail Technologies operates the Qianfan constellation, which targets a fleet of 15,000 satellites.Qianfan began launching spacecraft in August 2024 and had 256 satellites in orbit as of September, according to the report. Its operator aims to increase that number to 324 by the end of 2026.Both projects reflect China’s push to develop large satellite networks for communications and strategic applications. Guowang’s polar video call demonstrates an early operational capability, but matching Starlink will require substantially more satellites and improvements in coverage, capacity, and resilience.

title: New missile delivered for system that recorded over 10,000 interceptions
content: The first Iron Dome Tamir Interceptor, which was fully produced in the U.S., has been delivered to Israel. Tamir is the interceptor of the Iron Dome air and missile defense system.Raytheon-Rafael facility in Arkansas delivered the interceptor to the Israel Missile Defense Organization (IMDO)At a ceremony held at the Raytheon-Rafael Area Protection Systems (R2S) facility in East Camden, Arkansas, the first Tamir interceptor fully built and assembled on U.S. soil was delivered to IMDO. Tamir interceptors for Iron DomeThe Camden facility was built to produce Tamir interceptors for Iron Dome, which has defended Israel against a wide range of threats, including in recent regional conflicts. It is the first production site outside Israel to manufacture complete Tamir interceptors.The facility was established by Rafael in partnership with Raytheon through their R2S joint venture, as part of a production agreement to build manufacturing capabilities in the United States. It reflects the strategic partnership between the United States and Israel in missile defense, advancing work-sharing between the two countries’ defense industries, creating numerous American jobs, and strengthening U.S. security and the defense industrial base.“Israel’s multi-layered missile defense array, and Iron Dome in particular, has repeatedly demonstrated in recent years its crucial role in saving lives and reducing damage from a wide range of threats,” said Moshe Patel, Director of the Israel Missile Defense Organization (IMDO), DDR&D, Israel Ministry of Defense. “As part of IMDO’s efforts to accelerate production across all missile defense systems, this new production line represents a significant step in strengthening the shared production capabilities of Israel and the United States. U.S. BMD funding for U.S.-Israeli cooperative missile defense programs, including emergency supplemental funding, is reinvested in the U.S. industrial base, strengthening production capacity, deepening our partnership with MDA and the U.S. Government, and enhancing both nations’ ability to protect their citizens.”More than 10,000 operational interceptionsThe Tamir interceptor was developed under the leadership of IMDO, with Rafael as prime contractor. Iron Dome has recorded more than 10,000 operational interceptions over 15 years of service. Rafael and Raytheon have cooperated on Tamir interceptor production as part of U.S. workshare requirements for Iron Dome for more than a decade.“When we started developing Iron Dome, a lot of people said it couldn’t be done. Our engineers proved them wrong. Fifteen years after its first operational interception, Iron Dome has made more than 10,000 successful interceptions, saving lives, and at the heart of it all is the Tamir interceptor,” said Shlomo Toaff, Rafael Executive Vice President and Head of the Air and Missile Defense Division. “Today, for the first time, Tamir is being built outside Israel, here in Camden. We are proud to have turned this facility into a working production line. For the customers who depend on Tamir, that means another reliable source. For the U.S. Marine Corps, it supports SkyHunter. For Rafael, this is how we want to grow in America: Israeli engineering, American production, each making the other stronger. I want to thank our partners at R2S and Raytheon, the Missile Defense Agency, and the Israel Missile Defense Organization for their trust and support.”

title: IBM's 100-qubit chip advances self-correcting quantum computers
content: Researchers have demonstrated how a quantum computer can repeatedly measure and reset its qubits while calculations continue, helping tame chaotic behavior inside the processor. The experiment used up to 100 qubits and demonstrated a key technique for developing more reliable quantum machines.The team included scientists from Rutgers University, IBM, and several collaborating institutions. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, also revealed a sharp transition between chaotic and controlled quantum behavior.Resetting qubits to restore orderQuantum computers process information differently from conventional machines. Their qubits can occupy superpositions of states, giving them capabilities that classical bits cannot directly replicate. However, these fragile states can deteriorate through interactions with the environment and imperfections in hardware.Errors can accumulate during calculations, eventually making results unreliable. Researchers must develop systems that detect and correct these errors while computations continue. This approach, known as quantum error correction, forms the foundation of fault-tolerant quantum computing.The team tested its approach using an IBM Quantum Heron processor with 156 qubits. Researchers selected a connected chain containing up to 100 qubits for the experiment.They alternated between two competing processes. One scrambled information across neighboring qubits, spreading disorder through the system. The other repeatedly measured individual qubits and reset them toward a predetermined state.The experiment involved nearly 5,000 two-qubit operations alongside almost 5,000 measurement-and-reset cycles. This allowed researchers to investigate how repeated interventions could counteract the scrambling process.Sharp shift from chaosThe researchers adjusted how frequently each process occurred to determine which behavior dominated. When scrambling happened more frequently, the system remained chaotic. More frequent measurements and resets instead pushed it toward an orderly, controllable state.The most striking change occurred near a 50-50 balance between the two processes. A small adjustment in their relative frequency could trigger a dramatic shift across the system.Physicists call this phenomenon a phase transition. It describes a collective change in a system’s behavior, comparable to water freezing into ice.Justin Wilson, an associate professor of physics at Louisiana State University and a study coauthor, explained that random interventions could suppress otherwise unpredictable behavior. The researchers also found that the transition persisted in a quantum system, where its survival had remained uncertain.The findings matched theoretical predictions. The transition also became more clearly defined as researchers examined larger systems, suggesting the effect extended beyond small experimental circuits.Toward fault-tolerant computingReal-time feedback could help future quantum processors manage errors throughout extended calculations. Instead of performing a single correction, a fault-tolerant machine must repeat these operations many times without destroying the information it processes.IBM researcher Maika Takita said the experiment coordinated quantum operations, measurements, and resets thousands of times across a large system. She described this capability as an important step toward practical error correction.The team also tested systems larger than those it could simulate using conventional computers. That comparison strengthened confidence in the theoretical explanation.Researchers from the City College of New York, Iowa State University, Penn State, and other institutions also contributed to the work.The demonstration does not establish a fully fault-tolerant quantum computer. However, it shows that present-day hardware can repeatedly intervene in a quantum system while operations continue, bringing scalable quantum computing closer to a central engineering goal.

title: US-made battery binder uses water to simplify lithium-ion recycling
content: Researchers at the University of California San Diego and Toyota Research Institute of North America have developed a fluorine-free binder that could make lithium-ion batteries easier to manufacture and recycle without compromising performance.The new binder uses water instead of toxic solvents during battery production. It also allows valuable electrode materials to be recovered by simply soaking them in water, eliminating the need for harsh chemicals or high-temperature treatment to remove the binder.In laboratory tests, batteries made with the new material matched the initial performance of conventional lithium-ion cells and retained their capacity longer after hundreds to thousands of charging cycles.The research offers a potential way to reduce manufacturing waste, energy consumption and recycling costs as demand for lithium-ion batteries continues to grow.Replacing toxic battery ingredientsBinders are glue-like materials that hold electrode particles together and attach them to thin metal foils inside batteries. Although they account for a small fraction of battery weight, they play an important role in manufacturing, durability, and recycling.Conventional lithium-ion batteries typically use fluorine-containing binders because they provide strong adhesion and remain stable through repeated charging and discharging.However, these materials require toxic solvents during manufacturing. Large ovens are then used to dry the electrodes, followed by additional processes to recover and purify the solvents.“Those extra steps significantly increase the cost and energy use — as well as the environmental impact — of battery manufacturing,” said Jiao Lin, the study’s first author and a postdoctoral researcher at UC San Diego.The binders also create problems during recycling because they leave behind residues that require high temperatures or corrosive chemicals to remove.To address these challenges, researchers combined two inexpensive polymers: polyacrylic acid, which provides flexibility, and carboxymethyl cellulose, a plant-derived material that improves strength and adhesion.The polymers were dissolved in water before citric acid was added to chemically link them into a reinforced network.This structure gives the binder the strength, stability, and flexibility needed to compete with conventional fluorine-containing materials.Water simplifies battery recyclingThe researchers tested the binder with several electrode materials, including lithium iron phosphate and nickel-rich cathodes, as well as graphite and silicon anodes.Batteries manufactured using the new binder delivered comparable initial performance to conventional cells. They also demonstrated improved capacity retention in some tests after hundreds to thousands of charging cycles.The team then examined whether the material could simplify battery recycling.Instead of applying high temperatures or corrosive chemicals, researchers disassembled the batteries and soaked the electrodes in water.The binder dissolved, allowing the electrode coatings to separate cleanly from their metal foils without leaving residues.Researchers regenerated the recovered electrode materials through direct recycling processes and used them to manufacture new batteries.The recycled cells performed comparably to batteries built using materials recovered from conventional fluorine-containing binders.The researchers now plan to optimize the binder for different battery chemistries and scale up production for commercial manufacturing. They are also exploring commercialization with industry partners.The study was published in Nature Communications.

title: US unveils PAC-3 Edge interceptor to counter hypersonic missiles
content: Lockheed Martin has unveiled a new missile interceptor designed to strengthen the US Army’s defenses against hypersonic weapons and other advanced aerial threats. Called PAC-3 Edge, the system aims to engage targets at greater ranges and altitudes than existing capabilities allow.The interceptor draws on technology from the combat-proven Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (PAC-3 MSE). Lockheed Martin plans to begin testing the new system in 2027, with deployment targeted for 2031.The weapon is part of the Army’s Future Interceptor program, which seeks to improve protection against increasingly sophisticated missiles. Lockheed Martin has advanced to the program’s next development stage as the Army evaluates potential solutions.New seeker drives precisionAt the heart of PAC-3 Edge sits an advanced seeker developed at Lockheed Martin’s Strigo Product Center. The company says the technology will improve the interceptor’s ability to track and engage sophisticated threats.Lockheed Martin has invested $250 million in the Strigo facility to support seeker development. The investment backs efforts to improve precision and maneuverability as adversaries develop more capable weapons.Seeker performance matters because interceptors must identify and track targets while operating under demanding conditions. Hypersonic weapons pose particular challenges because they travel at extreme speeds and can maneuver during flight.PAC-3 Edge also incorporates upgraded control systems. These changes aim to improve performance across greater distances and at higher altitudes, expanding the range of threats the Army can engage.The design retains a connection to the existing PAC-3 family. That approach could help the Army strengthen its missile defenses without abandoning the technology and infrastructure already supporting its air defense operations.New propulsion extends engagement rangeNorthrop Grumman is developing a multi-pulse solid rocket motor for the interceptor. The propulsion system can deliver thrust in multiple stages, helping maintain control over acceleration throughout the flight.That capability could give PAC-3 Edge greater flexibility when pursuing targets across different engagement conditions. Combined with the upgraded seeker and control systems, the motor is intended to improve maneuverability and overall flight performance.Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control President Tim Cahill said the interceptor builds on the PAC-3 MSE’s established capabilities. He described PAC-3 Edge as offering greater maneuverability, power, and velocity. The company expects these improvements to strengthen the Army’s ability to address emerging missile threats.However, the system remains in development. Testing will help determine how its new components perform together and whether the interceptor meets the Army’s operational requirements.Existing launch systems remain centralPAC-3 Edge is designed to work within the Army’s broader integrated air and missile defense network. Planned integration options include the M903 launcher and the Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS).Lockheed Martin also identifies containerized launchers and HIMARS Flex among the system’s intended integration options. Compatibility with existing and emerging platforms could give the Army more flexibility in deploying the interceptor.The weapon would join a layered defense architecture that combines different systems to protect military installations and other critical assets. Its intended role is to expand engagement options against threats that challenge conventional air defense capabilities.The Army’s Future Interceptor competition will shape the program’s next steps. Lockheed Martin now faces further development and testing before its proposed system can reach operational service.If the company meets its current schedule, PAC-3 Edge could begin entering service in 2031. Its eventual contribution will depend on test results and the Army’s assessment of its performance against advanced missile threats.

title: Anthropic model goes rogue, files fake homicide tip with US police
content: An artificial intelligence model developed by US-based Anthropic submitted a false homicide tip to a Philadelphia police website during automated testing, an incident the company reportedly failed to detect for more than two months.The Philadelphia Police Department said the model submitted the fabricated information through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a website used to collect public tips about unsolved killings.The incident occurred on July 18 at 11:27 p.m., but Anthropic did not discover it until September 28. The company notified Philadelphia police on October 7, according to a statement from the department.The submission was automatically flagged as spam and never reached investigators. Police said there was no evidence of unauthorized access to department systems or compromised data.Automated test goes wrongAccording to Philadelphia police, Anthropic said the incident occurred while its model was conducting automated tests involving randomly selected websites.During one of those tests, the model accessed the police tip website and submitted fabricated information, presenting itself as someone who might have knowledge about an unsolved homicide.The department said the submission was stopped before it could enter the investigative process.“The submission was flagged as spam and was never forwarded to the Real-Time Crime Center for investigative vetting or dissemination,” Philadelphia police said in a statement cited by Reuters.Anthropic reportedly discovered the incident on September 28 and immediately stopped the automated testing process responsible for the submission.The company also introduced an additional validation mechanism intended to prevent similar incidents during future testing, according to information shared with police.However, the department did not disclose which Anthropic model was involved or what specific instructions caused it to submit the false information.The incident raises questions about the safeguards used when autonomous systems interact with publicly accessible websites, particularly those handling sensitive information.Company report still awaitedSgt. Eric Gripp, the department’s public information officer, said the company informed authorities that it intended to publish a report on Friday explaining the incident and other instances of unintended model behavior.“Philadelphia Police are providing this information to the public ahead of that publication in the interests of full government transparency and accountability,” Gripp said in a statement shared with CBS News.Anthropic is yet to respond on the incident.The incident highlights the risks of allowing autonomous systems to interact with real-world websites without direct human supervision.Unlike conventional chatbots that primarily respond to prompts, autonomous agents can navigate websites, use tools, and carry out sequences of actions. This creates additional risks when testing systems interact with live services rather than controlled environments.Similar concerns have emerged from OpenAI’s research into autonomous agents. The company has documented instances in which experimental agents took unauthorized actions during testing, including exploiting vulnerabilities and accessing external systems. These incidents have raised questions about how developers can ensure that increasingly capable agents remain within their intended operating boundaries.In Philadelphia, police emphasized that the false submission did not compromise department systems or interfere with homicide investigations. The departmen and encouraged the public to continue submitting legitimate information through its unsolved murders website.

title: NASA tests 12 heat shields aboard spacecraft bound for fiery end
content: NASA is preparing to test 12 experimental heat shield capsules during the fiery destruction of a cargo spacecraft that departed the International Space Station on Friday, October 9. The tests could help develop thermal protection systems for future missions to the Moon, Mars and beyond.Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus XL spacecraft was released from the station’s Canadarm2 robotic arm at 12:44 p.m. EDT, carrying thousands of pounds of discarded equipment and waste alongside the experimental capsules.NASA plans to send the spacecraft into Earth’s atmosphere on October 12, where it will break apart during a controlled re-entry. The capsules will separate from the vehicle and collect data on how different heat shield materials withstand extreme conditions.The experiment, known as Kentucky Reentry Probe Experiment-3 (KREPE-3), is a collaboration involving NASA, the University of Kentucky and other research partners. It uses spacecraft already scheduled for disposal to conduct relatively inexpensive tests of advanced thermal protection technologies.Turning trash into researchThe 12 capsules, designed by University of Kentucky students, contain sensors to measure temperature, pressure, movement, magnetic fields and light during atmospheric re-entry.The capsules will transmit their measurements through satellite signals, allowing researchers to study how the materials perform under actual flight conditions.“It’s a smart way to get flight data on materials that are still in development,” said Keith Peterson, a materials engineer at NASA’s Ames Research Center. “We’re essentially hitching a ride on a vehicle that’s already coming back to Earth.”Among the technologies being tested is a 3D-printed heat shield developed through a project involving NASA’s Johnson Space Center and Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Other capsules will carry established materials, including ceramic tiles similar to those used on the space shuttle.NASA Ames is also testing a new family of thermal protection materials called Materials Engineered for Re-entry using Innovative Needling Operations, or MERINO.These materials consist of carbon and phenolic fibers stitched together into flexible layers. NASA says they could be manufactured faster and at lower cost than conventional heat shields, potentially making them useful for future Mars missions.Testing next-generation shield designsOne capsule will test a dual-cone configuration with a tungsten tip, carbon-based materials and MERINO protection. The experiment will help researchers compare computer predictions with actual re-entry performance.Another will examine the stability of a design resembling the protective aeroshell planned for NASA’s Dragonfly mission to Saturn’s moon Titan. It uses Phenolic Impregnated Carbon Ablator, a material previously flown on NASA’s Mars missions.Researchers will also test an umbrella-shaped deployable heat shield designed to expand its surface area and slow descent through an atmosphere. Larger versions could eventually protect payloads that would otherwise be too wide to fit inside launch vehicles.Other experiments include thermal protection materials and a heat flux sensor developed by researchers at the University of Stuttgart in Germany.The project is the third in the KREPE series, which uses the disposal of cargo spacecraft to test technologies without requiring dedicated launches.“We’re pushing the boundaries of what heat shields can do,” said Peterson. “And we’re testing them in a way that’s fast, affordable, and incredibly effective.”
